messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Poisson regression model very slow - because of simplex groups of regressors?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Poisson regression model very slow - because of simplex groups of regressors?
messages.body_plain:
Bob,

For each of my groups of regressors which sum to one, I omit one of them in order to deal with this issue.  Eg if I have 7 regressors in a group which sum to one, I only use 6 of them.

Note that the parameters are not constrained to sum to one, only the regressors.

Julian

> Might it be possible to fix this by going to a (K-1)-factor

> in Stan are parameterized in the unconstrained space with (K-1) free

>

> >

> >
> > Warmup of 1,000 to 2,000 iterations seems to produce reasonable results thereafter (although with about one effective sample per 10-20 iterations).  It's not slow, but thankfully I can run a large number of chains in parallel, so it's not intolerable to get a good level of accuracy.  It makes debugging a pain though.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Question about Wiener Diffusion Model Distribution in rstan_2.7.0-2
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: Question about Wiener Diffusion Model Distribution in rstan_2.7.0-2
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Sorry I'm a little late to this party, I had a long summer of travel.  The reason we originally implemented the lower-bound hits as negative reaction times was to have a cheap way of encoding what is essentially a bivariate distribution (strictly positive RT and binary response).  Because both the RT and the outcome are random variables, the current implementation (with only one bound) isn't entirely satisfactory if at any point we want to generate random numbers from the distribution.

I always liked the negative-RT solution even though it's a little counter-intuitive.  I'd probably prefer it in Stan since it's how it works in JAGS... but the more conventional solution would be to make it actually bivariate, and let it operate on a [RT response] pair, where the first is a strictly positive real and the second is a boolean.

Joachim

On Tuesday, August 4, 2015 at 8:34:27 AM UTC-7, Marco Inacio wrote:
> Suppose for example the user does some manipulation in his/her data that should be strictly positive, but something goes wrong, and it gets negative, then the distribution should give him an error since negative time does not indeed exist.
>
> If you check the implementation of this distribution in R (same author as this one), the function has an argument resp = "upper"/"lower"/"both", even though, internally the function uses negative/positive responses.
>
> So I think that's the correct way of doing it, and in the future an extra argument for lower/upper/both responses can be added (with default to "upper"), but then this wouldn't be backward compatible if the function was accepting negative responses right now.
>
> On 2015-08-04 12:09 PM, Matt wrote:
> > Hi Marco,
> >
> > On Saturday, 1 August 2015 00:17:52 UTC-4, Marco Inacio wrote:
> > > I changed this (thus forcing y to be strictly positive) because there
> > > was no computational advantage in doing so and thought it would be
> > > potentially dangerous for users.
> >
> > I'm curious as to the potential dangers of not having y as strictly positive for the Wiener distribution?
> >
> > Matt

messages.body_plain:
FWIW, I had problems with changing the extensions in mac. It automatically hides file extensions. So my original file, which was mymodel.cpp got changed to mymodel.stan.cpp (although in the finder it looked like mymodel.stan). Going to file info -> show extension and changing it from there did the trick.

On Thursday, October 1, 2015 at 2:36:25 AM UTC+10, Eric Buhle wrote:
> Okay, well, now it looks like changing the model file extension to .stan does the trick, no directory move necessary. I'm truly baffled, though, because (1) I tried this very thing yesterday with no success and (2) I was running version 2.8.0 with .r model files for a while before it stopped working. If it's got something to do with temp files needing to be deleted or overwritten then I guess I've been looking for those in the wrong place. Oh well, I suppose I'll get over it. It does seem like it would be good to have this (new, apparently) file naming requirement stated explicitly in the help page for stan() under the file argument.
>
> Thanks to Ben and James for the help!

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Sum of lognormals?
messages.body_plain:
On Wednesday, September 30, 2015 at 1:41:07 PM UTC-7, Geoff Davis wrote:
> While I really like the declarative model building in Stan, it had me thinking about the problem in the wrong way.  I've enjoyed the philosophical discussion, and some of the comments spurred me to look at the problem a bit differently.  I think I've figured out what I need to do to move forward (but alas it involves writing my own MCMC code rather than using Stan).  Thanks, all!
>

Geoff, I did some thinking about this problem in comments over on my blog. But I'll give a summary over here:

let's ignore the weights for the moment and say that y is the sum of three variables

y = a + b + c

you declare

a ~ lognormal(...)
b ~ lognormal(...)

and then you want a likelihood p(y | a,b)

but c ~ lognormal(...) as well, and p(y | a,b,c) = delta_function(y-a-b-c).

so, to get p(y|a,b) you can marginalize away c...

p(y| a,b) = integrate(p_c(c) * p(y | a,b,c),dc) = integrate(p_c(c) * delta_function(y-a-b-c), dc) = p_c(y-a-b)

so:

y-a-b ~ lognormal(pc_parameters)

this is exactly the logic behind your model (1) and may well sample in Stan just fine if it stays away from the "edge of the world" since a,b,y-a-b all need to be positive.

I'd recommend trying to run your (1) and seeing what happens.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Sum of lognormals?
messages.body_plain:
On Wednesday, September 30, 2015 at 2:24:55 PM UTC-7, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> I still don't think Stan is "declarative" in any useful
> sense.  It uses imperative programming constructs (loops,
> conditionals, local variables, etc.), and uses them to define
> a log density, which it can then sample from.  That's really
> all Stan's doing.

It's not declarative in a programming sense, but it is declarative in a modeling sense. You "declare" the density you want to sample from, and it figures out how to do the sampling. It's a little like declaring the facts you know to prolog and then it figures out how (depth-first-search) to find the valid solutions to your problem.

So, in Stan, you don't describe the technique for getting the samples, you just describe the thing you want to sample from.

However, in Stan, the way you declare the density is to use iterative programming techniques to describe the density computation, so that's different from BUGS/JAGS for example where you declare the structure of a directed graph or whatever.

Daniel

messages.body_plain:
Yes, there is. My guess is that your initial time, t0, is 0.

The ts have to be sorted, unique, and all greater than t0, in this case 0. We need to document it better in the manual and the right thing to do is to relax that condition in the underlying C++ code.

Just in case you're wondering, the integrate_ode() call uses the implementation of the Runge-Kutta Dormand-Prince 5 method in Boost's ODEINT package. For the first implementation of our wrapper function, integrate_ode(), we followed the requirements of the Boost solver, which requires sorted, unique times which do not include the initial time. In order for us to make the Stan function more flexible, it's a lot of bookkeeping that can be done in C++, it's just tricky. (perhaps a little trickier than it looks on the surface because we're having to track the gradients and we do this with a coupled system. see the arXiv'ed math paper for details)

So, in short, you can set the 2nd to the nth element of y_hat by dropping the first ts. The first element of y_hat should be y0. Hopefully that helps.

Daniel

> Sorry I'm a little late to this party, I had a long summer of travel.  The reason we originally implemented the lower-bound hits as negative reaction times was to have a cheap way of encoding what is essentially a bivariate distribution (strictly positive RT and binary response).  Because both the RT and the outcome are random variables, the current implementation (with only one bound) isn't entirely satisfactory if at any point we want to generate random numbers from the distribution.
>
> I always liked the negative-RT solution even though it's a little counter-intuitive.  I'd probably prefer it in Stan since it's how it works in JAGS... but the more conventional solution would be to make it actually bivariate, and let it operate on a [RT response] pair, where the first is a strictly positive real and the second is a boolean.
>
> Joachim
>
> On Tuesday, August 4, 2015 at 8:34:27 AM UTC-7, Marco Inacio wrote:
> Suppose for example the user does some manipulation in his/her data that should be strictly positive, but something goes wrong, and it gets negative, then the distribution should give him an error since negative time does not indeed exist.
>
> If you check the implementation of this distribution in R (same author as this one), the function has an argument resp = "upper"/"lower"/"both", even though, internally the function uses negative/positive responses.
>
> So I think that's the correct way of doing it, and in the future an extra argument for lower/upper/both responses can be added (with default to "upper"), but then this wouldn't be backward compatible if the function was accepting negative responses right now.
>
> On 2015-08-04 12:09 PM, Matt wrote:
>> Hi Marco,
>>
>> On Saturday, 1 August 2015 00:17:52 UTC-4, Marco Inacio wrote:
>> I changed this (thus forcing y to be strictly positive) because there
>> was no computational advantage in doing so and thought it would be
>> potentially dangerous for users.
>>
>> I'm curious as to the potential dangers of not having y as strictly positive for the Wiener distribution?
>>
>> Matt

I have tried for several times since yesterday but the sampling stops at the 2nd chain each time. The code is below and stan files are attached. Hopefully someone can reproduce the phenomenon.

An unrelated question, to avoid recompiling the model, do we always need to first run fit <- stan() and then pass fit to stan for more iterations and chains? Or there is anyway to save the compiled model and load it later? Can anyone give me a link that I can follow?

```{r}
library(rstan)
rstan_options(auto_write = TRUE)
options(mc.cores = parallel::detectCores())
n <- 4 ## number of layers
N <- n+1 ## Number of yhats
theta <- c(kpwa = log(2)/100, kpse = log(2)/100, Kd = 50)
Zs <- 2
Zsed <- rep(Zs/n,n)
x_r <- c(rhob=2.05,theta=0.5,Zw=5,Dp=0.05,delta=1,Zsed)
fixpar <- x_r
y0 <- c(1,rep(0,n))
ts <- seq(1,100,by=10)
T <- length(ts)
t0 <- 0.0
## sm <- stan_model(file="WS4.stan")
swData <- stan(file="RPest/stan/WS4.stan",data=c("T","y0","t0","ts","theta","fixpar"),chains=1,iter=1,algorithm="Fixed_param")
y <- extract(swData,"y_hat")
ypred <- y$y_hat[1,,]
y <- cbind(ypred[,1],apply(ypred[,2:N],1,sum))
```

### Direct Optimization

```{r}
fit <- stan(file="WS4fit.stan",data=c("T","y","t0","ts","theta","fixpar","N"),chains=1,iter=1)
res <- optimizing(get_stanmodel(fit), data=c("T","y","t0","ts","theta","fixpar","N"),  hessian = TRUE)
res$par[c("M0","theta[1]","theta[2]","theta[3]")]
theta
sqrt(diag(solve(-res$hessian)))

```

### MCMC Sampling

```{r}

fit2 <- stan(fit=fit,data=c("T","y","t0","ts","theta","fixpar","N"),chains=3,iter=1000)
save(fit2,file="fit2.Rdata")
print(fit2)
plot(fit2)
```

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Dynamic linear regression with constrained coefficients
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Dynamic linear regression with constrained coefficients
messages.body_plain:
Sorry I missed replying to this one earlier.

Have you tried running for more than 1000 iterations?  Some models
take a while to warm up properly and it looks like you may just need
more time. This is especially true of models that are not very well
identified.  It looks like you're doing the right thing to identify
the softmax component, though, so I'm not sure why this is taking
so long.

Also, we strongly recommend running more than one chain to diagnose
non-convergence.

This:

>     for (i in 2:N) {
>       phiraw[i,k] ~ normal(phiraw[i-1,k],sigma_phi[k]);
>     }

can be vectorized for more efficiency as

  phiraw[i] ~ normal(phiraw[i - 1], sigma_phi);

And this

>  for (i in 2:N) {
>     alpha[i] ~ normal(alpha[i-1],sigma_alpha);
>   }

can be vectorized as

  tail(alpha, N - 1) ~ normal(head(alpha, N - 1), sigma_alpha);

and this

>  for (i in 1:N)
>   y[i]  ~  normal(alpha[i] + x[i]' * beta[i],sigma_y);

can be vectorized as

  y ~ normal(alpha + x * beta, sigma_y);

But you have to declare x as a matrix[N,3].  The data input
format won't change.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Sampling freezes at the 2nd chain.
messages.body_plain:
Does it just hang?  If so, I'm guessing what happens is that you
are getting into a stiff part of the ODE parameter space, which
Stan can't handle.  We have some patches in place undergoing testing
right now that should solve this problem partially for Stan 2.9 (a
few months out).  And then after that, we should have a stiff ODE
solver in place for Stan 2.10 early next year.

Until then, I don't have many suggestions other than to

1.  try initializing with reasonable values,

2.  try setting stepsize lower so you're less likely to step into
bad parameter values early on

3.  set target acceptance (adapt_delta) higher so you keep the
step size low and avoid getting into stiff regions later.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I will be presenting a 1 day workshop entitled "Getting Started with Bayesian PKPD Modeling Using Stan" at the American Conference on Pharmacometrics (ACoP) on 10/8/2015 in Crystal VA. While it is more introductory than appropriate for most of this group, I thought I should let you know of its existence. Of course I won't complain if you pass it on to colleagues who might be interested.

Cheers,

Bill

There are still open seats for our post-meeting workshop on Bayesian pharmacometric modeling using Stan. Go to the ACoP6 site (http://www.acop6.org/acop6-registration) to register.

Here’s a more detailed description of the workshop...
Getting Started with Bayesian PKPD Modeling Using Stan: Practical use of Stan and R for PKPD applications

Instructors: Bill Gillespie and additional Metrum Research Group scientists

Where & when: Hyatt Regency Crystal City, Washington Room; 8am - 5pm 8 October 2015

After a brief review of Bayesian principles and computation, we will provide a guided hands-on experience in the use of Stan (http://mc-stan.org/) for Bayesian PKPD modeling. Stan is a flexible open-source software tool for Bayesian data analysis using Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) simulation---a type of MCMC simulation. You will execute Bayesian data analysis examples using rstan, a R package interfacing R and Stan. Via the examples you will learn to implement nonlinear regression models, nonlinear mixed effects models and additional programming required for population PK models. The latter includes learning how to deal with dosing and observation event schedules, and with censored data, e.g., BQL data. We will discuss the pros and cons of Stan relative to other tools.

Full Price: $600

ISoP Members: $600

ISoP Member Students: $200

Academia/government attendees: $200

Materials provided by Metrum: Course slides, data and code for all examples, online access for one month to a cloud-based compute server on which the software used in the course is installed

Requirements for Attendees: Knowledge and experience in PKPD modeling, nonlinear mixed effects modeling and the use of R (or S-PLUS).  Basic understanding of Bayesian principles.

Participants should bring a laptop that meets the following requirements:

OS: Windows 7 or above, or OS/X 10.7 or above

Browser: Chrome, Firefox, Safari or Internet Explorer 10+

Internet access via Wi-Fi.

Workshop outline

Introduction to Bayesian statistical principles and methods

Bayes Rule

Bayesian modeling & inference process

Computation for Bayesian modeling

Key challenge of Bayesian modeling and inference: sampling from high-dimensional probability distributions

General computational approach: posterior simulation

Brief intro to Markov chain Monte Carlo simulation

Stan basics

What is it?

How do I get it?

How do I run it?

Using rstan

Stan demo: Linear regression

Introduce PK/PD modeling case study to be used throughout the course

Hands-on example 1: Simple nonlinear regression

Topics in Bayesian model development using Stan I

R tools for running Stan and analyzing MCMC simulations

Assessing convergence

Programming hierarchical models (aka mixed effect or population models)

Hands-on example 2: Nonlinear mixed effects

Topics in Bayesian model development using Stan II

User-defined functions

Programming for pharmacometricians:

PK models

Dosing and observation event schedules

Why Stan?

vs ML tools (NONMEM, Monolix, Phoenix, nlme/r, etc.)

vs BUGS variants (WinBUGS, OpenBUGS, JAGS)

Parallel computation with rstan

Hands-on example 3: Population PK.

Additional topics & closing discussion

Dealing with censored data in Stan, e.g., BQL data

Optimizing Stan code

What can you do in Stan that you can’t do with your current tools?

What didn’t we cover?

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] few desired features for Rstan
messages.body_plain:
The thing to do is create feature-request issues in
GitHub.  Project (1) is for Stan, project (2) for RStan.
They have different GitHub repos and issue trackers.

1.  I'm not sure what the feature is here.  A new function?
A rewrite of the existing neg_bin_rng?

Assuming that neg_bin_rng is the result (I wouldn't call it that,
since I take an RNG to be a random number generator, not
a random draw), in one case it's an integer and in the
other it's real.  Is there some kind of truncation?

Stan's data type only goes up to int for integers, so
that maxes out at 2^31.  We put our bound where we did
so as to be able to handle the whole of range of
poisson_rng.

To avoid that, you can do the test yourself for values
that are too large.  Or you can sample outside of Stan.
If the mean's too large, then you wind up expecting draws
that are too large to fit in an int anyway.

Do you want to assign a real value to the result in a
different function?

Extend Stan's int to long?  This would be great, but it's
a big project.

2.  I'll leave that to the folks who know about R and/or Windows.

- Bob

> On Oct 3, 2015, at 11:03 AM, Linas Mockus <linasm...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi,
>
> I would like to add some simple features to some future release of Rstan (there are workarounds of course).
>
> 1. I have been struggling with neg_binomial_2_log_rng for a long time.  While the chains converge during warmup the error is thrown up because the parameter for the underlying poisson_rng is too large.
> Ben suggested the following excellent workaround:
>
>   if (is_inf(theta))
>     gamma_temp <- nu;
>   else
>     gamma_temp <- gamma_rng(theta, theta / nu);
>   if (gamma_temp < poisson_max)
>     neg_bin_rng <- poisson_rng(gamma_temp);
>   else
>     neg_bin_rng <- normal_rng(gamma_temp, sqrt(gamma_temp));
> Another alternative is to allow generated quantities block to be executed only during sampling.
>
> 2. It is nice to see the progress of parallel chains not only in Internet Explorer but also as text file. Below is the workaround I came with by using previous postings. The output of all chains is redirected to one outfile.
>
> par.stan <- function (file, code, data, warmup, n.draws, chains, pars,
>     init, outfile)
> {
>     # compile C++ code
>     sm <- stan (file = file, model_code = code, data = data, chains = 1,
>         iter = 0)
>     CL <- makeCluster (chains, outfile = outfile)
>     clusterExport (cl = CL, c ("data", "pars", "warmup", "n.draws"))
>     sflist <- parLapply (CL, 1 : chains, fun = function (cid) {
>         require (rstan)
>         stan (fit = sm, data = data, chains = 1, warmup = warmup,
>             iter = n.draws + warmup, pars = pars, init = init,
>             chain_id = cid)
>     })
>     stopCluster (CL)
>     if (chains == 1) {
>         return (sflist [[1]])
>     } else {
>         return (sflist2stanfit (sflist))
>     }
> }
> stanmod <- function (chain, file, sm, data, warmup, n.draws, pars, init) {
>     if (length (init) == 1) {
>         if (init == "random") {
>             init <- "random"
>         } else {
>             init <- list (init [[chain]])
>         }
>     } else {
>         init <- list (init [[chain]])
>     }
>     sampling (sm, data = data, pars = pars, chains = 1,
>         iter = warmup + n.draws, warmup = warmup,
>         init = init,
> #        diagnostic_file = diagnostic_file,
> #        sample_file = sample_file,
>         verbose = TRUE, refresh = max ((warmup + n.draws) / 10, 1),
>         chain_id = chain)
> }
>
> Thanks,
> Linas
>
>

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Lagrange Multipliers for contraints?
messages.body_plain:
Tam, Bob, everybody,

I was into coding a bayesian support vector machine (bSVM) in STAN. In their dual form
in common to use lagrange multiplier to cope with the inequality condition.

I looked in the group here and thought maybe somebody else know how to handle
contraints. I found:

https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/CFbIiXAzHl0/mSRKER0WNcoJ

So I tried to make it very simple and put the lagrange example in the STAN optimizer.
You all right. I doesn't makes sense.

Just for informational background:

I have had the idea to use STAN as an Bayesian optimizer.
Currently we do optimizing like an optimizing tunnel.
We pick on point, optimize and get one result.
We do that repeatedly. At the end of the other side
we get a 'picture'.
But what, if we could transmit whole distributions
through the "tunnel"?
Our solver have constraints. So how could I had constraints
to STAN. Thus I come up with the Lagrange multiplier idea.
To make it more practical, in the company I worked before,
we had a simulation of the factory. We did a simulation,
picked one state out of the simulation process, optimized
that. Repeated that n-times and then at the end we
reviewed the optimized points.

Andre

> Does it just hang?  If so, I'm guessing what happens is that you
> are getting into a stiff part of the ODE parameter space, which
> Stan can't handle.  We have some patches in place undergoing testing
> right now that should solve this problem partially for Stan 2.9 (a
> few months out).  And then after that, we should have a stiff ODE
> solver in place for Stan 2.10 early next year.
>
> Until then, I don't have many suggestions other than to
>
> 1.  try initializing with reasonable values,
>
> 2.  try setting stepsize lower so you're less likely to step into
> bad parameter values early on
>
> 3.  set target acceptance (adapt_delta) higher so you keep the
> step size low and avoid getting into stiff regions later.
>
> - Bob

Hi!

I was just wondering under what conditions I can go with a diagonal (unit) mass matrix: To my understanding, the diagonal of the mass matrix should be the variances of my parameters in the posterior. So if I have good reasons to assume that I know beforehand the variances of my parameters in my posterior, then I could scale my variables and skip a lot of effort during warmup right?

What would left to be done during warmup? I.e. assuming the above works, what is the least number of steps during warmup to get likely good sampling parameters?

Thanks!

Best,
Sebastian

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] warmup for the lazy
messages.body_plain:
We've rarely seen any performance gain with a dense
mass matrix.

When we estimate the mass matrix, we use the inverse of
a regularized sample covariance from the last half of the
draws from warmup in exponentially increasing block sizes.
There's a description in the part of the manual about algorithms.

The other piece of warmup is step size tuning for the target
acceptance rate.  That's it --- once you have those, there's
nothing else.  So yes, that could conceivably save all of your warmup.
Or you could give it a good starting point and let it work from there.
But that might not work as set up because we have to go from wherever
the initialization is at to the typical set (high mass volume of the
posterior), and the curvature may vary.

We're going to let users specify mass matrix plus step size, either fixed
or as initializations, but right now, there's no way to input them in any
of our interfaces.

Scaling variables so they're all unit scale in the posterior would
eliminate the need to estimate a mass matrix --- you could use the unit mass
matrix.

- Bob

> On Oct 5, 2015, at 8:04 AM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi!
>
> I was just wondering under what conditions I can go with a diagonal (unit) mass matrix: To my understanding, the diagonal of the mass matrix should be the variances of my parameters in the posterior. So if I have good reasons to assume that I know beforehand the variances of my parameters in my posterior, then I could scale my variables and skip a lot of effort during warmup right?
>
> What would left to be done during warmup? I.e. assuming the above works, what is the least number of steps during warmup to get likely good sampling parameters?
>
> Thanks!
>
> Best,

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] few desired features for Rstan
messages.body_plain:
Ben's function returns real values (normal_rng), whereas neg_binomial_2 and
poisson return integers.  In Stan, those can only go up to 2^31
on the positive side, so anything much outside the bounds we
have set now can't generate values we can represent in Stan's precision.

Once we're up in the 2^30 (1 billion) range, the integer rounding's probably
not going to matter much, but we can't handle the overflow.

It would totally make sense to extend Stan's integer type to long.
Then we could just extend the precision on our discrete RNGs.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Lagrange Multipliers for contraints?
messages.body_plain:
I don't know much about either Lagrange multipliers or Bayesian
optimization.  Stan is only able to do MCMC, variational inference,
and optimization.

Constraints on variables need to be implemented in Stan through transfroms
from R^N to a suitable natural space for modeling (usually a constrained
portion of R^M, for M >= N).  An example is mapping any point in R^N to a
simplex in R^(N+1) using softmax (we use a stick-breaking construction, but
the idea's the same).

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: Lagrange Multipliers for contraints?
messages.body_plain:
On Friday, October 2, 2015 at 1:41:03 PM UTC-7, andre.p...@googlemail.com wrote:
> Hi,
>
> I read various post about contraints, and come up to the idea to
> use Lagrange Multipliers in STAN. See example 1 in:
> https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagrange_multiplier
>

Lagrange multipliers are more or less an analytic technique (ie. if you are trying to solve analytically for locations where derivatives vanish), they aren't necessarily appropriate directly for numerical usage.  A related technique is "penalty" methods. If you are willing to put up with "soft" constraints g(x) \approx 0, you can take f(x) + K*(g(x))^2. The contribution from g(x) is obviously is minimized when g(x) = 0. When K goes to infinity the solution to this penalized minimization procedure is equal to the constrained minimum of f(x) subject to g(x)=0. But this is not always a practically effective method.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Using of log predictive density rather than log posterior for measuring predictive accuracy
messages.body_plain:
The posterior is a distribution over _parameters_ so it doesn’t tell you
anything about prediction.  Prediction is defined by new measurements,
which means you need a distribution over _measurements_.  So
mathematically the posterior isn’t even applicable.

Really the only distribution over measurements that we have are the
distributions defined in the likelihood, but to make a prediction we
need to narrow this down to a single distribution.

In frequentist methods one selects a single “best” parameter and then
uses the corresponding distribution, L(data | theta_best), to make
predictions.  This is especially common in machine learning.

>From a Bayesian perspective we can average over the likelihood.
Using the prior gives the prior predictive distribution,

p_{prior predictive} (data_new | data_meas) = \int dtheta L(data_new | theta) p(theta).

This was used by George Box back in the day but has some pathologies
that limits its use.  Instead it’s much more robust to average over
the posterior to incorporate what we’ve learned into the prediction,

p_{post predictive} (data_new | data_meas) = \int dtheta L(data_new | theta) p(theta | data_meas).

This is the formally correct “posterior probability for a new data point”
and is the basis for posterior predictive checks, WAIC, etc.

If warmup could be improved - that would be great!

One advantage of somehow figuring out the scale and then re-scaling variables would be that this information can be saved across many runs. Redoing the warmup over and over again is very wasteful. Does the performance of Stan degrade substantially if I scale with a somewhat "too large" scale than what would be optimal? If so, then one could scale to this and somewhat relax the requirements on initialization.

Yet another approach would be to use an approximate scheme first, define with this a proposal density, then do full Bayes and finally re-sample using IS.

these uses in the language section of the manual, following
Gelman and Hill's regression book's classification of variables.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] warmup for the lazy
messages.body_plain:
> On Oct 7, 2015, at 3:45 AM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> If warmup could be improved - that would be great!
>
> One advantage of somehow figuring out the scale and then re-scaling variables would be that this information can be saved across many runs. Redoing the warmup over and over again is very wasteful.

The motivation for multiple runs is to make sure we
converge from diffuse starting points.  That means redoing
warmup.

> I know, that this also requires sensible inits as other wise things go wrong which makes it a chicken - egg problem.

The chicken and egg problem is that adaptation is often
required to find the typical set, but you want to adapt
only to the typical set after you find it.  That's why we
only use the second half of warmup iterations to train the
mass matrix (reduces to variable scaling with the default
diagonal mass matrices).

> Does the performance of Stan degrade substantially if I scale with a somewhat "too large" scale than what would be optimal?

Yes.  It can cause the integrator to be so bad that
Stan devolves to random-walk Metropolis.  Erring on the
too-small side is much safer in that it's less likely
to kill the flow that makes HMC so efficient.

>  If so, then one could scale to this and somewhat relax the requirements on initialization.
>
> Yet another approach would be to use an approximate scheme first, define with this a proposal density, then do full Bayes and finally re-sample using IS.

There's lots of open research to do out there.  And
we have a nice way to evaluate it with our modeling
language in case anyone wants to do it.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
We typically think of lp__ as just one more quantity of interest.  Poor convergence on an quantity of interest represents poor convergence in the distribution.  (If any man anywhere is a slave, none of us is free.)   So I think you have poor mixing here.

>

Stan computes the ESS for the log posterior (LP), and I was wondering if there is there any literature that talks about being able to use this LP ESS as some sort of measure of overall sample quality as we do for parameter ESS.

messages.body_plain:
Okay, thanks very much. I'll have to chew this over a bit.

But just to be clear: this is supposed to be a model with random intercepts (county-level intercepts b0, hyperparameters B0) and effects fixed across counties (beta). b0 is thus C x J (outcome categories x counties), B0 is length C, and beta is K x C (parameters x outcome categories). So beta can't be J x C. I don't know if this changes your diagnosis.

To put a little meat on the bones: These are felony cases, sampled from 12 counties in CA, in which defendants either (1) plead to a felony, (2) go to trial, (3) plead to a misdemeanor, or (4) have their cases dropped. Fun stuff, right?

It might help to see a BUGS model that works (sloooowly):

> > model{
> > # level 1 model
> > # create multinomial data
> > for (i in 1:N){
> >   for (c in 1:C){
> >     y[i,c] <- equals(adjout[i],c) ;
> >     }}
> > # likelihood
> > for (i in 1:N){
> >   for (c in 1:C){
> >     eta[i,c] <- beta0[id[i],c] + beta[1,c] * cblack[i] +
> >     beta[2,c] * clatin[i] + beta[3,c] * sapred[i] +
> >     beta[4,c] * detain[i];
> >   expeta[i,c] <- exp(eta[i,c]) ;
> >   mu[i,c] <- expeta[i,c]/sum(expeta[i,1:C]) ;
> >   }
> >   # distribution of y
> >   y[i,1:C] ~ dmulti(mu[i,1:C],1)
> >   }
> >
> > # level 2 model

> > for (j in 1:J){

> >   beta0[j,1] <- 0;
> >     for (c in 2:C){
> >       eb0[j,c] <- B0[c] ;
> >       beta0[j,c] ~ dnorm(eb0[j,c], tau_b0[c]) ; }}
> >
> > # priors
> > B0[1] <- 0 ;
> > for (c in 2:C){
> >   B0[c] ~ dnorm(b0_prior[c-1], 1.0E-2) ;
> >   }
> >
> > tau_b0[1] <- 0 ;
> > for (c in 2:C){
> >   tau_b0[c] <- pow(sigma_b0[c], -2) ;
> >   sigma_b0[c] ~ dunif(0, 5) ;

> >   }
> >
> > for (k in 1:K){

> >   beta[k,1] <- 0.0 ;
> >   for (c in 2:C){
> >     beta[k,c] ~ dnorm(0.0, 1.0E-2) ;
> >     }}
> > }

Thanks again for Stan and for your patient advice.

Best,
John

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] warmup for the lazy
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

Currently, Stan always starts from scratch which is a safe choice, but waste the information we already have. Modeling proceeds by altering the model (most of the time in small steps) and by altering between smaller and larger data sets (to do fast model build-up and then have once in a while a "full" but slow run).

Hence, both processes (model build-up) and data alteration can be viewed as a perturbation to what one has. As a consequence, the perturbed system by which I refer to parameters and tuning parameters will be within the vicinity of where we already are. Therefore, there is no need to start from scratch again - which saves a lot of time. Of course, one needs to be aware of the dangers such an approach entails, i.e. starting from scratch once in a while is an important consistency/stability check of the model.

To some degree I can take advantage of the above thought be being "informative" with the initials, doing so with the tuning parameters is the logic next step and it is great to hear that this is on its way.

But, I see, I am jumping ahead of what is in the works.

Sebastian

In which case it could help to start the adaptation at a reasonable point.  Currently we can give inits to Stan. It will be good when we can also give Stan the tuning parameters.

messages.subject: Re: What do these warnings mean?
messages.body_plain:
On Thursday, October 8, 2015 at 5:45:27 AM UTC-4, UD1989 wrote:
> I'm getting these warnings I've never seen before.

These warnings weren't thrown prior to 2.8.0 but the behavior was probably the same (i.e. not good).

> The results/ parameter distributions look ok and as expected, so I do not know If I am even suppossed to act on these?:

Yes.

> Warning messages:
> 1: There were 2000 transitions after warmup that exceeded the maximum treedepth. Increase max_treedepth.
> 2: Examine the pairs() plot to diagnose sampling problems

You should specify control = list(max_treedepth = 15) in the call to stan() or some other number greater than 10 to allow the sampler to make more leapfrog steps per iteration. When it hits the maximum treedepth, you essentially cannot get from one part of the parameter space to another part of the parameter space in one iteration, which increases the dependence among the draws and may bias the draws relative to the true posterior distribution. The problematic points are shown in yellow if you call pairs() on the stanfit object but in this case, it looks as if all the transitions are problematic.

Ben

People can abuse MCMC against our recommendations at their own risk.
We don’t have time to police bad statistics — we also don’t have to facilitate it.

On Oct 7, 2015, at 1:19 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:

> That’s Betancourt-bait for sure!
>
> > On Oct 7, 2015, at 5:13 AM, Julian King <jking...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > I have a very long Stan run with lots (16 chains).  One of the chains became stuck.  I would like to excise this chain from the stanfit object, and hopefully maintain the resulting object as a valid stanfit object.  Failing that, I just want the output of summary().  How can I do this?  I am using Stan 2.8 via RStan.
> >
> > I realise the caveats around doing this (MCMC must work all the time, not just for certain initialisations / sampler parameter values), but I'm willing to bear that risk at present.
> >
> > Thanks in advance!
> >

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] log posterior effective sample size question
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] log posterior effective sample size question
messages.body_plain:
This is a really tricky issue and it requires being somewhat pedantic about MCMC estimators.

The first thing to keep in mind is that autocorrelation and effective sample size are all dependent
on the choice of a function.  Yes the entire distribution of the Markov chain is converging to the
target posterior,

T^{n} delta_{0} -> pi

but we have no way to measuring that.  So instead we monitor how expectations are converging,

1/N sum_{n = 1}^{N} f(x_{n}) -> E_{pi} [ f ],

with the f-dependent autocorrelation and effective sample size.  One consequence of this is that
expectations of some functions converge faster than others — for example the expectation of a
constant converges immediately!  Intuitively, the more a function varies the more sensitive it will
be to fine detailed structure in the posterior and hence slower it will be to converge.  So seeing
variation in the effective sample sizes (including the log posterior density which we can consider
as just another function) is not technically pathological.

But then comes the second consideration — we don’t know the autocorrelation and effective
sample size exactly and we have to estimate them.  Estimating autocorrelation is really, really
hard, especially when the autocorrelations are large.  One consequence of this is that when
expectations are converging really slowly the autocorrelation and effective sample size estimators
are typically huge overestimates.  Consequently, seeing variation in the effective sample sizes
can be due to poor estimators.

So which is it?  Well in practice we’ve seen the latter more than the former which, combined with
our perpetual yet friendly skepticism of MCMC, makes us take low log posterior density ESS
seriously.  But like so many MCMC diagnostics it’s not always a pathology so we’d require more
details to say more.

Sorry for the ambiguity, doing MCMC well is hard!

messages.body_plain:
You can't assign arrays, like theta, to vectors like Y[1].

So you just want to bind them together, so what you want is
this:

parameters {
  row_vector[N] a;
  row_vector[N] b;
}
transformed parameters {
  matrix[2, N] ab;
  ab <- append_row(a, b);
}

You can declare ab as being matrix[N, 2] if you
declare a and b as vector and use append_col.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Obtain gradient inside model section
messages.body_plain:
Yes, very tricky.  The problem isn't the recursion per se,
so much as the staging.  Our reverse-mode autodiff for gradients
builds up the entire expression graph then propagates the chain
rule backward.  So the derivatives aren't available until after
the entire expression's built up and derivatives are propagated,
at which point, the model block's already been executed.

Going the other way, we'd very much like to be able to add in
a way for users to specify gradients for custom functions.

- Bob

I'm afraid I didn't understand the question.  You can
always include prior knowledge in a Bayesian model.  If you
have uncertainty in a parameter, integrate over it (usually
by sampling).  As to calibrating vs. true uncertainty, you
can't just use simulation --- you need real data to assess things
like overdispersion of real data relative to a model.

> If the median of the posterior is around 0.17, you shouldn't set

In general we prefer soft constraints.  Use hard constraints when they are an intrinsic part of the model (for example, a correlation that has to be between -1 and 1). Use soft constraints to encode prior information and to induce regularization.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] sample size predictive posterior
messages.body_plain:
There’s no generic way of doing “sample size” calculations in
a Bayesian setting because the posterior concentration can
vary dramatically with the actual data measured.  Considering
the worst case (for example minimum shrinkage) moves one
into the direction of Probabilistically Almost Correct (PAC)
methods that sort of have sample size equivalents.  But really
if your posterior isn’t in the exponential family (in which case
you can do the usual methods) then there’s no “right” answer.

On Thursday, October 8, 2015 at 9:31:48 PM UTC+8, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Thursday, October 8, 2015 at 5:45:27 AM UTC-4, UD1989 wrote:
> > I'm getting these warnings I've never seen before.

> > The results/ parameter distributions look ok and as expected, so I do not know If I am even suppossed to act on these?:

> Yes.
>
> > Warning messages:
> > 1: There were 2000 transitions after warmup that exceeded the maximum treedepth. Increase max_treedepth.
> > 2: Examine the pairs() plot to diagnose sampling problems
>
> You should specify control = list(max_treedepth = 15) in the call to stan() or some other number greater than 10 to allow the sampler to make more leapfrog steps per iteration. When it hits the maximum treedepth, you essentially cannot get from one part of the parameter space to another part of the parameter space in one iteration, which increases the dependence among the draws and may bias the draws relative to the true posterior distribution. The problematic points are shown in yellow if you call pairs() on the stanfit object but in this case, it looks as if all the transitions are problematic.
>
> Ben
>

messages.subject: Hierarchical phylogenetic regression problems
messages.body_plain:
Hi stan users,

I am having a lot of trouble with a multi-level model that I am helping a colleague with. I am trying to model individuals of several tree species' responses to nitrogen and phosphorous and then model the species responses to nitrogen as a function of several plant traits. The model is essentially a direct copy of the  multivariate regression example from the stan manual (pp 64-69). The only difference is that at the second level, the multivariate normal VCV matrix is being multiplied by a phylogenetic correlation matrix. This correlation matrix has a lambda parameter multiplied to the off-diagonals to estimate the "strength" of phylogenetic history's effects on the regression (between 0 & 1). The model works well enough when the higher level just  contains an intercept term, but once I add another level of predictor variables, mixing becomes horrible and I get lots of divergence warnings. I am worried I messed up the math but haven't been able to figure out what's wrong. Any advice would be greatly appreciated! Ultimately I would like to estimate the trait means for each species from the data (which have missing values), but at the moment I can't even get the model to work when the trait means are fixed as data.

The model and data are included as attachments. My session info is listed below.

Thanks so much for any help!

Best,

Zach Marion

Sorry --- that's indeed very confusing.

Integration time (int_time) is stepsize * L,
where L is the number of steps.  So

  L = int_time / stepsize

But specifying int_time and stepsize is confusing becuase
L has to be an integer.  I don't know  what happens if
int_time / stepsize has a non-zero remainder.

The reason for the int_time specification is that you want
to choose the time to be long enough to allow a trajectory to
get around the posterior, and then for that time, choose the stepsize
as large as is stable.

messages.body_plain:
You just do something like this:

parameters{
…
vector[L-2] z;
}

transformed parameters {
  vector[L] x;
  for (i in 1:41) x[i] <- z[i];
  for (i in 42:65) x[i] <- z[i-1];
  for (i in 67:100) x[i] <- z[i-2];
  x[41] <- 1;
  x[66] <- -1;
}

model {
  z ~ normal(0,1);
…
}

Or something like that.  I might be mangling the syntax, also this is a bit of an ugly way to do it, but you should get the general idea.
A

messages.subject: conceptual question-multilevel regression
messages.body_plain:
Hello All

I am using STAN for a multilevel hierarchial bayesian regression model. I have two 'levels'- say 'items' and 'Product_category' . There are many transactions within a item type and there are may items within a 'Product_category'.  There are 3 predictors in my input matrix. Usually, the model works well with the data. However, there are some (rare) cases where the item type has the same value throughout for one of the predictors (as in the 'size' property of the transactions is 100 metres throughout). In ths case the beta(posterior distribution corresponding to size) is wrongly calculated in absence of any variation in my predictor.This is ofcourse kind of expected-however I believed that the whole point of using a hierarchial bayesian model is that the model will 'draw' information from the level-2 of the hierarchy and hence there will be  constraint to what values beta can take. This isnt happenning. Pretty sure I am doing something remarkably stupid---so any help is appreciated on this :)

Thanks and Regards

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,
I'm using the WAIC measure to compare the goodness of fit of some model. For some of them, the WAIC is negative. I don't understand how I can interpret such a result.
Any idea ?
messages.body_snippet:
Dear all,
I'm using the WAIC measure to compare the goodness of fit of some model. For some of them, the WAIC is negative. I don't understand how I can interpret such a result.
Any idea ?

messages.subject: Re: Negative WAIC
messages.body_plain:
It is not necessarily a problem for WAIC or any other criterion to be negative. The same thing happens with AIC. Smaller is still better.

WAIC is scaled like deviance, and deviance is scaled as -2 log-probability. For a continuous probability density, like Gaussian, it is easy for deviance to be negative. Consider for example:

-2*dnorm(0.1,0,0.1,TRUE)

messages.subject: Re: Negative WAIC
messages.body_plain:
Like Richard says, it's fine for it to be negative. There's nothing good or bad about a negative value, it just happens to be negative, like in Richard's example. The particular values you get for different models are not what's of interest but rather how those values relate to each other.

On Monday, October 12, 2015 at 10:14:57 AM UTC-4, Richard McElreath wrote:
> It is not necessarily a problem for WAIC or any other criterion to be negative. The same thing happens with AIC. Smaller is still better.
>
> WAIC is scaled like deviance, and deviance is scaled as -2 log-probability. For a continuous probability density, like Gaussian, it is easy for deviance to be negative. Consider for example:
>
> -2*dnorm(0.1,0,0.1,TRUE)

I have a simple question about thinning chains in Stan. I'm using CmdStan, but I think this applies to other interfaces too.

Suppose I thin my chains, and there sometimes is a n_divergent error. Will I be able to see this from the output - or will I only see it if the n_divergent occurs in the iterations that have not been thinned?

Alternatively, is there a way of summing up the n_divergent along the way?

-op

Thinning is always a bad idea in that it loses information.

And usually people set the number of effective samples higher
than they need for their inferential purposes.

ten bytes per real in ASCII), or 8GB for 1000 iterations.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Cholesky factor isn't triangular (rstan 2.8)
messages.body_plain:
Where did the error occur?  This may be due to changes
in the Eigen library's use of the unfilled part of a matrix.
You could probably fix the problem directly by filling in
the upper triangle of LG with 0 values.  We'll look into
it if you can verify where you're getting the error.

But this is probably all irrelevant for the problem at hand.
You shouldn't need to Cholesky decompose a diagonal matrix
and go through the elaborate multiplication of X with blups.

  SG <- diag_matrix(rep_vector(s2g, G));
  LG <- cholesky_decompose(SG);
  blups <- LG * blupsStd;

I'm pretty sure this reduces to just this:

  blups <- diag_matrix(rep_vector(sqrt(s2g) * blupsStd, G));

And then you can further simplify be eliminating
X * blups in favor of just:

  yHat <- mu + X * sqrt(s2g) * blupsStd;

At least I think I got the algebra right.

- Bob

messages.subject: Quantile Regression
messages.body_plain:
Dear List,

Quantile regression has come up once <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/stan-users/%22quantile$20regression%22/stan-users/DUv_uFFedCM/Y5KgALJqbP4J> or twice <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/stan-users/%22quantile$20regression%22/stan-users/uvj_WNQQM_Y/NgSvxSbmCAAJ> before, but I can't seem to find a reproducible example of anyone who's got it working.

The only MCMC code I can seem to find online is this example <http://stats.stackexchange.com/a/17717> from a JAGS model, based on a data augmentation procedure described by Reed & Yu (2009 )[1].

I've converted it to Stan code (.Rmd file attached, and on GitHub, here <https://github.com/brendan-R/quantile_regression/blob/master/quantile_regression.Rmd>, html output here <https://rawgit.com/brendan-r/quantile_regression/master/quantile_regression.html>), and compared the results to the JAGS output, and results from the bayesQR and quantreg R packages.

Unfortunately I'm getting whacky results out of Stan. I can't seem to get the model to converge, and the coefficients look pretty far off. My questions:

> 1. Can anyone spot a problem in my Stan code? Some of the warning messages are unexpected. For example, I'm getting warnings that the exponential distribution function is being fed negative values, which shouldn't be possible (tau is constrained to be positive, as far as I've understood my own code).
>
> 2. Could it be that this particular algorithm is only suitable for Gibbs sampling? (From skimming the paper, it seems like this may be the case, however, I'm no expert!)
>
> 3. If this quantile regression algorithm is peculiar to GIbbs sampling, what procedure, if any, might be appropriate for Stan?

I'm keen to use Stan (as opposed to falling back to JAGS/Gibbs), as the final model I'd like to fit is QR on-top-of a large hierarchical model.

A minimal reproducible example of quantile regression would be an excellent addition to the Stan list/manual!

Best,

Brendan

Reed, C., & Yu, K. (2009). A Partially collapsed Gibbs sampler for Bayesian quantile regression.
URL: http://bura.brunel.ac.uk/bitstream/2438/3593/1/fulltext.pdf

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] generated quantities only after warmup?
messages.body_plain:
Yes, generated quantities are executed during warmup.  Otherwise, there's
no way to produce plots, etc.  It's a bit of a pain because if the generated
quantities crash during warmup, it stops sampling.

The way you could have tested this would be to set up something that
only does warmup and include a print statement.

- Bob

P.S.  That should say "once per iteration" not "once per sample".
Andrew's been on me not to conflate a sample (a set of draws)
with a single draw, but it's still making its way through all of
our broken doc.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Nonparametric variational inference
messages.body_plain:
Hi Marmaduke,

great question. There’s been a lot of recent work that extends beyond this framework. In general, using a mixture of Gaussians as an approximation makes it very difficult to optimize in a robust and easily accessible manner (e.g., how many mixtures, does nonparametrics make sense, is the computation efficient?). Rajesh Ranganath, David Blei, and I are working on a very similar idea that uses recent tricks from the literature. It extends the variational model to arbitrary mean-field distributions + prior. This means you can fit both discrete and continuous latent variable models, and the approximation can be made as accurate as you want it to be.

It should go up on arXiv soon, and we’re all (Alp included) excited about its future for ADVI.

Best,
Dustin

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Nonparametric variational inference
messages.body_plain:
One more comment:

I think the main challenge to implementing NPV in Stan is that it makes use of the diagonal of the Hessian of the log-posterior. There are ways to compute or approximate this efficiently, but none are implemented in Stan at the moment (to my knowledge).

In any case, Dustin's points are quite relevant; in particular, NPV only optimizes an approximate bound (in general), and in very high dimensions the benefits to using a mixture diminish, since it gets harder to fill up the space with Gaussians. I'm excited to see what Dustin, Rajesh, and Dave come up with as an alternative :)

Matt

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] conceptual question-multilevel regression
messages.body_plain:
Your hierarchical model doesn't have a hierarchical variance component.
That's what would control posterior variance.  Instead, you've
hardcoded the value 10.

Also, it looks like the pooling is backwards.  You have:

>  for (j in 1:J)
>     a[j]~ normal(0, sigma_a);

>   for (j in 1:J)
>     beta[j] ~ normal((u[j] * gamma), 10);
>
>   for (n in 1:N) {

>   y_hat[n] <- a[condolist[n]] +beta[condolist[n]][1] * x[n,1] +beta[condolist[n]][2] * x[n,2] +beta[condolist[n]][3] * x[n,3];

The prior for a looks OK (though it should be vectorized),
but you're pooling the parameters for each group beta[j,] rather than
pooling across groups, than beta[,1], beta[,2], and beta[,3].

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Nonparametric variational inference
messages.body_plain:
We do not have an efficient way to compute just the diagonal
of the Hessian.  The fastest would probably be N passes of
fvar<fvar<double>> forward-mode autodiff.  That'd be O(N^2),
because there are O(N) passes and each log posterior will
presumably cost O(N) [it'll be worse for models like dense GPs].

How's the diagonal then used?

This is an issue for Riemannian HMC with the diagonal
Hessian approximation.  There, the motivation is in part to avoid
all the solver cost on the N x N matrix, and compared to O(N^3),
O(N^2) doesn't look so bad (N passes which assume the
log posterior calc is itself O(N)).

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] generated quantities only after warmup?
messages.body_plain:
> On Oct 13, 2015, at 5:07 PM, Guido Biele <guido...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thanks for the info,
>
> the problem isn't that anything is crashing, but that I calculate average predictive comparisons in the generated quantities. This is very slow because it involves computing pairwise comparisons between data points. Therefor I would have liked to avoid computing them during the warmup.
>
> I believe I once read a request to expose the iteration number so that it could be used to determine which section of a program is executed. But if I remember correctly this was not implemented because there were reasons not to do this.
>
> So in conclusion it looks as if I just have to live with the fact that the generated quantities block is also executed during warmup.
>
> Is this correct?

Yes it is.

The reason not to remove values from warmup iterations
is that if they're not there, all of our posterior tools
will crash and burn.

The reason we don't want to expose iteration number and/or
chain ID is that it's not part of the log density abstraction
we've made --- we think of a Stan model plus data as being
something that given uncontrained parameter values, computes
log density and gradients.  If we add things in the language
th pick out iteration numbers, then we have to hack them in
places where there aren't iterations, such as when used
in diagnostics or in external calls from R.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
At a high level, the diagonal in NPV is used to do a sort of approximate Laplace approximation.

The only way I know of to efficiently automatically compute the diagonal of the Hessian is using repeated symbolic differentiation; there may be a way to do it with reverse-mode automatic differentiation, but if so it'll be pretty hairy.

BTW, for a lot of models (e.g., GLMs) the cost of computing the Hessian is O(MN^2), where M is the number of observations; if M>N, then there's not much point in worrying about the O(N^3) cost of solving a big system of equations.

Matt

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] generated quantities only after warmup?
messages.body_plain:
I agree with Ben!

If I find that i have a stable model (i.e. a model that converges well),
I tend not to save the warmup samples/iterations.

I'll just add an issue to the stan repository and hope for the best ;-).

Just to give an example of how burdensome unnecessary calculation
of the generated quantities can be when calculating average predictive comparisons (APC)*:

Lets assume one does a multiple regression with 5 predictor variables and n=1000.
To do APCs one calculates for each predictor variable all pairwise comparisons
of the y_hats for all cases (I am simplifying a bit here...). This means next to 2.5 million
pairwise comparisons per sample/iteration.
Unfortunately, my analyses involve around  20 predictors and 40000 cases.
So even though I am doing a hierarchical model and the number of pairwise comparisons
is reduced because comparisons happen only within subgroups, a lot of
pairwise comparisons are calculated in the generated quantities block.

Therefor the possibility to turn of calculation of generated quantities when
warmup samples/iterations are not saved would be very much appreciated.

Guido

*www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/ape17.pdf <http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/ape17.pdf>

Cheers - Guido

messages.subject: Mixing two models together dramatically increases sampling time
messages.subject_clean: Mixing two models together dramatically increases sampling time
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have a ordered categorical model, that takes about 20 second for 200 sampling iterations. I want to put a known covariate matrix into it to describe cross correlations between observations. I have 600 observations, so the covariate matrix will be 600 by 600. With Cholesky factoring, this multivariate normal model itself takes about 20 seconds for 200 sampling iterations.

However, after putting the multivariate model into the ordered categorical model, the sampling time increase to about 15 mins. So, we are talking about from 20+20 seconds to 15 mins, a 22 times increase in terms of sampling time simply by mixing two models together. Is this normal? Are there anything to improve this?

More details: the ordered categorical model and 7 parameters to estimate, the multivariate_normal itself has 600. Putting together has 607. This raises another conceptual issue, especially on the multivariate normal model, with 600 observations, and 600 parameters to estimate, is this incur the degree of freedom issue as in the frequentist point of view? Seems the bayesian side does not have this issue, but I am not clear.

I have attached my stan model.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] warmup for the lazy
messages.body_plain:
On Thursday, October 8, 2015 at 12:56:25 AM UTC-7, Sebastian Weber wrote:
> Hi!
>
> Currently, Stan always starts from scratch which is a safe choice, but waste the information we already have. Modeling proceeds by altering the model (most of the time in small steps) and by altering between smaller and larger data sets (to do fast model build-up and then have once in a while a "full" but slow run).
>
> Hence, both processes (model build-up) and data alteration can be viewed as a perturbation to what one has. As a consequence, the perturbed system by which I refer to parameters and tuning parameters will be within the vicinity of where we already are. Therefore, there is no need to start from scratch again - which saves a lot of time. Of course, one needs to be aware of the dangers such an approach entails, i.e. starting from scratch once in a while is an important consistency/stability check of the model.
>
> To some degree I can take advantage of the above thought be being "informative" with the initials, doing so with the tuning parameters is the logic next step and it is great to hear that this is on its way.

One possibility is to do your run with normal warmup, get your posterior values, and then rescale your model, and provide the rescaled posterior mean values as the initial positions for doing further runs with your extra data or perturbed model. The goal would be at least to reduce the number of warmup samples since you'd probably be starting in the typical set, and you'd have a mass matrix that's closer to a unit diagonal.

This is more or less just an efficiency hack, but it could be a big one. One thing I've definitely found is that when I build my models in dimensionless form to begin with and use my knowledge to rescale the variables so that they are all O(1) my Stan models run without many hitches. If you don't have info about your variable's scales, a single initial run of Stan could get you the info you need to rescale your model.

This is kind of the dual process to inputting an initial mass matrix, alter the model via pure rescaling so an initial unit diagonal mass matrix is already a good starting point.

messages.body_plain:
I didn't understand your model.  Why are you Cholesky decomposing
the Kinship matrix and then multiplying it by a parameter?

The model combo behavior is not unusual.   Sampling time is different than
function evaluation time.  When you combine models, the geometry
can get much more difficult to navigate.  What you'll see is that
the tree depth is going up.

The ordered categorical is tricky.

I take it you mean covariance matrix, not covariate matrix (which I'd probably
call "data matrix").  Did you try fitting with modeling covariance?

What happens when you get too many degrees of freedom is that you need
to control the posterior with priors.  Check out the problematic posteriors
chapter of the manual for a simple example.

- Bob

P.S.  I'd strongly recommend not coding the model as a string in R.  You
won't be able to decode line numbers in error messages and you either have
to escape transpose or quote, depending on how you marked the string in R.
Then it can't even be cut and paste out of R.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Nonparametric variational inference
messages.body_plain:
Multimodality is hard --- an open research problem.  There
are very simple multimodalities that standard approaches
can sample through all the modes for, some multimodalities which
are just nuisances, and then some special algorithms which can handle
limited multimodality.  Nothing can handle combinatorial multimodality
of the kind you get in models like LDA or Ising systems --- non-parametric
generalizations only make matters worse combinatorially.

- Bob

>

>
> 2) less effective in high dimensions in the multivariate sense (dense cov) or even for independently distributed variables (diag cov)?
>
>
> I have had some success with Stan/ADVI with a nonlinear dynamical systems model, but it appears to fail compared to sampling where the transition density (x[t+1] ~ normal(f(x[t], sig)) is multimodal.

messages.body_plain:
What I'm going to work on next after general indexing (almost done!)
is something to let you run a Stan model, then run a second generated
quantities block on the output.  Hopefully we'll then be able to put
the two things together into a single output, but that's an interface
issue more than an underlying Stan sampling issue.

Turning off generated quantities could work if no warmup draws
are saved.  In fact, we probably should do that as a matter of course.
The only time it could hurt is if you have a bad generated quantities
block, spend a long time in warmup only to discover there's a bug
in the generated quantities.

If 99% of your work's done in generated quantities and you
ran with half warmup, half sampling iterations, you'd save 49.5%
of the time not executing generated quantities during warmup.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
hi marmaduke,

that's a very interesting model.

do you remember what value of eta you used? i wonder if mean-field
might give you some more reasonable answers with a smaller value for
eta. (it'll take more iterations to converge, of course.) [we will be
releasing an auto-tuning feature for eta soon.]

i'd also be curious to see how fullrank does on a subset of the data.
(maybe the first T=100 points?) we found fullrank to perform really
well in the stochastic volatility model from the Stan manual, while
meanfield struggled to capture some aspects of the model.

we're very interested in structured covariance matrix approximations,
such as low-rank, sparse, banded, etc. i don't believe we have a
schedule for when we'll get around to exploring these options, but do
let us know if you'd be interested in implementing and/or playing
around with them!

cheers
alp

On Wed, Oct 14, 2015 at 2:01 PM, marmaduke woodman
<marmaduk...@univ-amu.fr> wrote:
> On 10/14/2015 07:28 PM, Alp Kucukelbir wrote:
>>
>> could you share some more details about your nonlinear dynamical systems
>> model?
>
>
> It's a model of a network of nonlinear oscillators with linear additive
> noise, coupled with a given connectivity matrix. Observations are a linear
> combination of the state variables. We encode the model like a
> autoregressive process, with a Euler-Maruyama discretization of the SDE,
> something like
>
> data {
>   matrix[N, N] weights;
>   matrix[S, N] gain;
>   matrix[T, S] Z;
>   real dt;
> }
> parameters {
>   matrix[T, N] X, Y;
> }
> model {
>   vector[N] input;
>
>   for (t in 1:(T-1)) {
>     input <- weights * X[t]';
>     X[t+1] ~ normal(X[t] + dt * dXdt(X[t], Y[t], input), sig);
>     Y[t+1] ~ normal(Y[t] + dt * dYdt(X[t], Y[t]), sig);
>     Z[t+1] ~ normal(gain*X[t+1]', eps);
>   }
> }
>
> where d{X,Y}dt are functions defining the differential equations, N is
> around 15 network nodes, and the current dataset has T=1000 time points, so
> the number of hidden states is in the tens of thousands. Still, we are
> seeing somewhat plausible results with the mean-field algorithm in a few
> minutes.
>
>> were you able to try it with the "fullrank" version of the algorithm
>>
>> (assuming your model/dataset is small?)
>
>
> It runs, but slow (10s of seconds / iter) and memory intensive (~ 8gb). I
> didn't wait for it to finish so I don't know if this is worth doing or not.
> FWIW, NUTS/HMC spends hours and hours warming up on the same model & data.
>
> At least for the sequence of hidden states, one would expect short-time
> correlation, so this made me wonder if some comprise between full rank and
> diagonal is possible, i.e. a banded or sparse covariance?
>

> Sorry to bring this thread up again, but why do we have:

> t_uncensored[n] ~ weibull(r, exp(-beta[group_uncensored[n]] / r));

Wasn't that the same question Jiqiang answered last time?  I'm appending
his original response, which hopefully has the clues you need to sort
it out.

- Bob

>From Jiqiang:
---------------

If we were able to specify a vector lower bound in stan, we would have

 t_censored[n] ~ weibull(r, exp(-beta[group_censored[n]] / r));

where t_censored are parameters and are defined as

real<lower=censor_time> t_censored.

But we cannot do the above, so a t2_censored is defined with lower bound 1.  Essentially,
t2_censored = t_censored / censor_time

Then the distribution of t2_censored needs to be derived from the distribution of t_censored and that is why the second argument of the weibull distribution is divided by censor_time.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Brendan,

Looking at the stan code there are several things that would lead to some problems.

1) Constraints need to be declared for everything that has constraints in parameters and transformed parameters. For example, if w has an exponential distribution then it needs to be positive so you need

vector<lower=0>[N] w;

and same for pe in transformed parameters, since it's also constrained to be positive.

2) We don't recommend hard constraints like lower=0.001, upper=10 for scale parameters. Better to declare sigma just to have lower=0 and then use a soft constraint imposed by the prior.

3) Also regarding pe, it looks like you're treating it the same in the Jags code as in the Stan code, but for Stan the normal distribution is parameterized in terms of the standard deviation whereas (if I remember correctly) Jags uses the precision.

4) We also don't recommend priors like normal(0,100) unless that big of a scale actually makes sense. Here you'd be better off using a much smaller scale for the normal priors on alpha and beta, e.g. normal(0,5) or even normal(0,1).

With those changes let us know if Stan gives better answers! Hope that helps,

Jonah

messages.body_plain:
That's very elegant --- like the sum to 0 constraint,
only more subtle.

I would like to warn you that this will ensure the constraint
is satisfied for any X in the data you use to fit the model, but
it won't necessarily satisfy the constraint out of sample.
You will need to look deeper into where the constraint comes from for that.

Alternatively, use exp(beta * X) instead of (beta * X) --- that's
guaranteed to be positive.   It's what you usually see in things like
Poisson GLMs that require positive linear predictors.

- Bob

and the error message you're getting?

You can't do col(beta, k) here because beta isn't a matrix,
it's an array of vectors.

  vector [M] beta[J];  //indiv. coeff by group

But assuming you make it a (J x M) matrix, then col(beta, m)
will be a size J column vector.

  matrix[J, L] u; //group predictors

  matrix[L,M] gamma; //group coeff

But then (u * gamma) is going to be a (J x M) matrix, so I'm not
quite sure what your intent is here.  But we definitely don't allow
matrices in the first argument position of a normal.

And then I don't see a sigma in the last model I found.

You basically have to set up the parameters block such that the inequality constraint is satisfied by construction, rather than relying on the fact that Stan will reject proposals for the parameters that happen to not satisfy the inequality constraint. I would try to basically do the same approach:
Solve for the value of some scalar parameter that renders y(X+dX,Z) - y(X) <= 0 for all observations with equality for one observation
Use that value for an upper or lower bound on that scalar parameter in the parameters block so that y(X+dX,Z) - y(X) < 0 for all observations

You may have to write a function in the functions block that implements (1) because you can't define any intermediate quantities in the parameters block.

Ben

> On Oct 15, 2015, at 11:09 AM, Guido Biele <guido...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hello,
>
> I am working with a zero-inflated negative binomial model in which I so far
> loop through cases as shown in the stan language reference.
> here is a snippet from the model block.
> (I am leaving out the other parts of the model, which essentially follow
> the example model for a hierarchical model with multivariate priors
> from the stan documentation )
>
> for (n in 1:N) {
>     theta_n <- dot_product(sx0[n],alpha);
>     eta_n <- dot_product(sx[n],beta[g[n]]);
>     phi_n <- phi[g[n]];
>     if (y[n] == 0)
>       increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(bernoulli_logit_log(1,theta_n),
>                              bernoulli_logit_log(0,theta_n)
>                              + neg_binomial_2_log_log(y[n],eta_n,phi_n)));
>     else
>       increment_log_prob(bernoulli_logit_log(0,theta_n)
>                    + neg_binomial_2_log_log(y[n],eta_n,phi_n));
>   }
>
>
> There are some things I could do to vectorize, but I am
> uncertain if this would lead to a noticeable speed improvement.
> Maybe somebody with the relevant knowledge can comment on this?
>
> Please note that I did not test this code, so there are nearly certainly bugs in it.
>
> A)
> split cases according to zero and nonzero outcomes (y)

Good idea to let you vectorize the y[n] > 0 cases.

> B)
> Loop through zero y (because of the need to use log_sum_exp),
> but use vectorization for nonzero y (I know this doesn't improve
> the speed of increment_log_prob, but hope it makes
> neg_binomial_2_log_log faster ...).

Exactly --- that's the only advantage of splitting them.

You can fully vectorize both ways efficiently like this:

   y_nonzero ~ neg_binomial_2_log_log(y, eta_n, phi_n)

   increment_log_prob(size(y_nonzero) * bernoulli_logit_log(0,theta_n)

where y_nonzero are the nonzero observations.

You could calculate the y_nonzero blocks in transformed data,
but we don't have a lot of convenience functions for this kind
of data manipulation.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: matrix with a single row
messages.body_plain:
Matlab doesn't have separate data type for matrix and vector, so when you are forming the data structure in Matlab it guesses the type based on the size, but it can't guess what you mean here, and so you need to explicitly specify that you want a matrix.

Here's an example were xt is specified to be 2-dimensional matrix, and yt is specified to be 1-dimensional vector
datcv=struct('p',p,'N',N-1,'Nt',1,'x',x(ii,:),'y',y(ii),'xt',{{x(cvi,:) 2}},'yt',{{y(cvi) 1}});

It's a bit kludgy and it's not yet documented (Brian?)

Aki

Jan

messages.body_plain:
On Saturday, October 17, 2015 at 1:45:52 PM UTC-4, dqsIJan Tünnermann wrote:
> Up to now I have been drawing the subject level versions all from normals, as described before for the C_n.
> Do the different types imply any better group level distributions? (I have the feeling that what you describe below may be good for the rate type parameters).

I don't really know anything about this research area and what is the best distribution to use would depend on the data. The computational principles I was trying to emphasize are that --- among parameterizations that yield the same marginal posterior distributions for the parameters of interest --- you generally want the primitive parameters to all have unit scale and to be independent of each other a priori. That is what the Matt trick does for unrestricted variables from a location-scale family. That is not straightforward if the variable is restricted to be non-negative, because, at a minimum, you induce a lot of prior dependence between the location parameter and primitive parameters that are being scaled so that the resulting variable is non-negative. You could assume that the non-negative parameter is lognormal and do Matt trick stuff on the log scale. Or you can use a variety of non-negative distributions (like the exponential) that are closed under rescaling but do not have a location parameter. There are some other options but the other computation principle is that you want to avoid using the declared bounds on transformed parameters to reject proposals for the primitive parameters that imply a transformed parameter is negative.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Frontier estimation using a quadratic function.
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Frontier estimation using a quadratic function.
messages.body_plain:
Identifying three parameters of a quadratic function is no problem.
That's just a regression.  For that, all you need to do is declare
x and y as vectors, a, b, and c as scalar (real) parameters,
sigma as a positive-constrained parameter, and do this:

  y ~ normal(a + b * x + c * x^2, sigma);

That then gives you a quadratic with symmetric normal noise scaled
as sigma.

But what you seem to want to do is solve an optimization
problem with a data-driven constraint.  So you seem to want the noise
to be asymmetric above and below the estimated value.  There's not
a neat way to do this that requires the noise to be positive (that is,
the curve picked out by a, b, and c to produce values for x below
observed values for y [or vice-versa]) that I can see in Stan.

- Bob
