messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Matt trick reparametrization question
messages.body_plain:
The utility of parameter expansion is usually limited to Gibbs samplers
and I’d be surprise if it proved useful here.  You really want to use
non-centered parameterizations (the more formal name of the “Matt trick”).

The trick is to decouple hierarchical parameters with a transformation.
For example, the standard parameterization

theta ~ normal(mu_pop, sigma_pop)

is bad because the group-level thetas are highly correlated with both
mu_pop and sigma_pop.  But if you do

theta_tilde ~ normal(0, 1)
theta = mu_pop + sigma_pop * theta_tilde

then theta_tilde becomes independent of mu_pop and sigma_pop,
yielding a nicer posterior.

You can do this for all kinds of distributions, but you’ll have to work
out the necessary transformations yourself.  For example, with an
exponential you could go from

theta ~ exponential(lambda_pop)

to

theta_tilde ~ exponential(1)
theta = lambda_pop * theta_tilde.

In practice I usually stick with generalized linear models, so leave
the thetas unconstrained and then constrain them using link functions,

theta_tilde ~ normal(0, 1)
theta = mu_pop + sigma_pop * theta_tilde
rho = exp(theta).

On Oct 17, 2015, at 12:22 PM, Jan Tünnermann <je...@mail.upb.de> wrote:

> Dear Ben,
>
> thanks again for the input. It really helps me to better understand what's going on. Probably the Matt trick thing is not suited for the group level parameters. I will try some sort of parameter expansion instead.
>
> Best regards
> Jan
>
> On 17.10.2015 20:21, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> > On Saturday, October 17, 2015 at 1:45:52 PM UTC-4, dqsIJan Tünnermann wrote:
> > > Up to now I have been drawing the subject level versions all from normals, as described before for the C_n.
> > > Do the different types imply any better group level distributions? (I have the feeling that what you describe below may be good for the rate type parameters).
> >
> > I don't really know anything about this research area and what is the best distribution to use would depend on the data. The computational principles I was trying to emphasize are that --- among parameterizations that yield the same marginal posterior distributions for the parameters of interest --- you generally want the primitive parameters to all have unit scale and to be independent of each other a priori. That is what the Matt trick does for unrestricted variables from a location-scale family. That is not straightforward if the variable is restricted to be non-negative, because, at a minimum, you induce a lot of prior dependence between the location parameter and primitive parameters that are being scaled so that the resulting variable is non-negative. You could assume that the non-negative parameter is lognormal and do Matt trick stuff on the log scale. Or you can use a variety of non-negative distributions (like the exponential) that are closed under rescaling but do not have a location parameter. There are some other options but the other computation principle is that you want to avoid using the declared bounds on transformed parameters to reject proposals for the primitive parameters that imply a transformed parameter is negative.

messages.body_plain:
This can be framed as a form of density estimation —
essentially the data are drawn uniform from below the
quadratic and exponential above it.  What you have to
be careful with are the normalizations — you can’t just
define a “distance function” you have to define a well-posed
probability density over probability densities (i.e. over the
parameter {a, b, c} which define probability densities over
the data).

Once you’ve done that you can run Stan to get a posterior
distribution over these probability densities.

On 10/18/2015 02:06 AM, Michael Betancourt wrote:

> The utility of parameter expansion is usually limited to Gibbs samplers
> and I’d be surprise if it proved useful here.  You really want to use
> non-centered parameterizations (the more formal name of the “Matt trick”).
>
> The trick is to decouple hierarchical parameters with a transformation.
> For example, the standard parameterization
>
> theta ~ normal(mu_pop, sigma_pop)
>
> is bad because the group-level thetas are highly correlated with both
> mu_pop and sigma_pop.  But if you do
>
> theta_tilde ~ normal(0, 1)
> theta = mu_pop + sigma_pop * theta_tilde
>
> then theta_tilde becomes independent of mu_pop and sigma_pop,
> yielding a nicer posterior.
>
> You can do this for all kinds of distributions, but you’ll have to work
> out the necessary transformations yourself.  For example, with an
> exponential you could go from
>
> theta ~ exponential(lambda_pop)
>
> to
>
> theta_tilde ~ exponential(1)
> theta = lambda_pop * theta_tilde.
>
> In practice I usually stick with generalized linear models, so leave
> the thetas unconstrained and then constrain them using link functions,
>
> theta_tilde ~ normal(0, 1)
> theta = mu_pop + sigma_pop * theta_tilde
> rho = exp(theta).
>
> On Oct 17, 2015, at 12:22 PM, Jan Tünnermann <je...@mail.upb.de> wrote:
>
> > Dear Ben,
> >
> > thanks again for the input. It really helps me to better understand what's going on. Probably the Matt trick thing is not suited for the group level parameters. I will try some sort of parameter expansion instead.
> >
> > Best regards
> > Jan
> >
> > On 17.10.2015 20:21, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> > > On Saturday, October 17, 2015 at 1:45:52 PM UTC-4, dqsIJan Tünnermann wrote:
> > > > Up to now I have been drawing the subject level versions all from normals, as described before for the C_n.
> > > > Do the different types imply any better group level distributions? (I have the feeling that what you describe below may be good for the rate type parameters).
> > >
> > > I don't really know anything about this research area and what is the best distribution to use would depend on the data. The computational principles I was trying to emphasize are that --- among parameterizations that yield the same marginal posterior distributions for the parameters of interest --- you generally want the primitive parameters to all have unit scale and to be independent of each other a priori. That is what the Matt trick does for unrestricted variables from a location-scale family. That is not straightforward if the variable is restricted to be non-negative, because, at a minimum, you induce a lot of prior dependence between the location parameter and primitive parameters that are being scaled so that the resulting variable is non-negative. You could assume that the non-negative parameter is lognormal and do Matt trick stuff on the log scale. Or you can use a variety of non-negative distributions (like the exponential) that are closed under rescaling but do not have a location parameter. There are some other options but the other computation principle is that you want to avoid using the declared bounds on transformed parameters to reject proposals for the primitive parameters that imply a transformed parameter is negative.

messages.subject: Re: Zero-Inflated Negative Binomial
messages.body_plain:
Hi Kenneth,

A few tips:

1) You want to use neg_binomial_2_log_log instead of neg_binomial_2_log. The names are unfortunate, but the former allows you to keep your linear predictor on the log scale. We really need to change the names because neg_binomial_2_log does seem like what you want but you need the extra _log at the end.

2) In your simulations you say that z is the logit regressor but in your model both x and z are used in the negative binomial rather than the bernoulli. Typically you'd use the same predictors (x in this case) in both calls to the negative binomial distribution and use z in a model for the bernoulli parameter theta. To do this, theta doesn't need to be declared as a parameter (just d0 and d1) and then you can construct theta in the model block, since it would be a deterministic function of d0, d1 and the data z. On a related note, I noticed that that the d0 and d1 parameters don't factor into your simulations of the data. I would generate z from a normal distribution and then compute inv_logit(d0 + d1 * z) and use that as the probabilities for the bernoulli in your simulations instead of just taking z from a uniform(0,1).

3) For both theoretical and computational reasons we recommend much tighter priors than normal(0,500), which gives non-negligible weight to values like -1000 and 1000. For your example you probably don't need anything wider than normal(0, 5), and you could probably even go tighter than that.

Hope that helps,

Jonah

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Complex hierarchical model --- any hints?
messages.body_plain:
Hi, here are some quick thoughts:
1.  We recommend putting the Stan program in a separate .stan file rather than encoding it as a character string.  That’ll be easier when you want to fit the model more than once.

2.  Hard constraints on parameters are typically a good idea.  Inherent constraints (such as sigma>0) are fine, but constraints such as <-.2,.2> are typically a badd idea.  Better to use a prior, for example replacing a hard <-.2,.2> constraint by a prior such as N(0,.1) or N(0,.2).
3.  Similarly for the parameter you bound between 0.01 and 0.99.  If it can’t be 0.995, it probably is highly unlikely to be 0.985.  Etc.
4.  No need to write 0 and 8 as 0.0 and 8.0.
5.  The Cauchy priors could be a bit weak.  I suggest replacing by normal or something like t_3 or t_7 if you want some long tails.
I suspect that none of these tips will solve your problem, but who knows?  Maybe!  I’m thinking it can’t hurt to put in some priors.
A

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Complex hierarchical model --- any hints?
messages.body_plain:
Dear Andrew,

thanks for the quick reply.

On 10/20/2015 01:17 AM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> Hi, here are some quick thoughts:
> 1.  We recommend putting the Stan program in a separate .stan file rather than encoding it as a character string.  That’ll be easier when you want to fit the model more than once.

Great, I was already wondering how to make use of that feature (because
I read people talking about fitting models without recompiling).

> 2.  Hard constraints on parameters are typically a good idea.  Inherent constraints (such as sigma>0) are fine, but constraints such as <-.2,.2> are typically a badd idea.  Better to use a prior, for example replacing a hard <-.2,.2> constraint by a prior such as N(0,.1) or N(0,.2).

OK, I'll try that. I must admit I was using the uniform ranges becaue I
can imagine the range from which samples are drawn more intuitively.

> 3.  Similarly for the parameter you bound between 0.01 and 0.99.  If it can’t be 0.995, it probably is highly unlikely to be 0.985.  Etc.

That's true. The idea was to not put in any information (which I
probalby still do) but avoid extreme values that may lead to problems in
the functions ...
These parameters are acutally biases between 0 and 1 that are neutral at
0.5. Is there any prior distribution favorable for such cases?

> 4.  No need to write 0 and 8 as 0.0 and 8.0.

I always do so if a language allows it. Can avoid hard-to-find erros is
statically typed languages. Also helps me to keep track whether there is
a continous range or discrete integer values.

> 5.  The Cauchy priors could be a bit weak.  I suggest replacing by normal or something like t_3 or t_7 if you want some long tails.

I think you may be right here. I have been following the advice from
your (2003?) paper on priors for variance parameters.Hence the Cauchys.
But I observed in the posteriors that the sigmas of many variables look
rather normally distributed.

The problem is, I have little feeling for how informative certain priors
(or contraints) may be. For simpler models in JAGS I just had it
generate prior predictive distirbutions by running the model without
data. I'm not sure if that is an option here as well.

> I suspect that none of these tips will solve your problem, but who knows?  Maybe!  I’m thinking it can’t hurt to put in some priors.

> A

Thanks again,
Jan

>> On Oct 19, 2015, at 7:09 PM, Jan Tünnermann <je...@mail.upb.de> wrote:
>>
>> Dear all,
>>
>> I'm still having trouble with non-efficient sampling in my hierarchical model (I already tried some things, see earlier e-mails). Intriguingly, often all four chains behave nicely except one. Or suddenly, out of nowhere, a chain get trapped for a long period.
>>
>> I prepared a simplified* version of this model and attached it. Maybe someone can have a quick look if there are some obvious mistakes. We haven't been working with Bayesian statistics for too long and especially I switched only recently to Stan (in the hope HMC can better deal with this model).
>>
>> The general structure of the model is as follows (in bottom-up order):
>> - on the stimulus level layer: positive outcomes are binomially distributed at each level
>> - on the subject layer: a custom psychometric function describes the success rates at different levels
>> - on the group layer: parameters of the mentioned function are drawn from normal group distributions
>>
>> Many thanks and best regards
>> Jan
>>
>> * I made the following simplifications:
>>    - deleted model structure of a second identical condition
>>    - deleted a huge generated quantities block, mostly containing differences between the two conditions
>>    - included dummy data within the script. Only 10 data sets are included, whereas the model is intended to run on 20+ data sets eventually. With half the data it is even more stubborn ...

Hi all,

I run into this issue after upgrading to 2.8.0

In my code, I use stan_model (<file_name>, model_name = <some char>, verbose=F) to create/compile the stan model and hold it in a variable.

I would then call sampling (<var_name>, data=<some list>) to run the sampling.

Since upgrading to 2.8.0, i noticed a 0 size file in created in temp when I run sampling (with cores.=1 and I have also explicitly passed in open_progress=F, show_messages=F) for chain exectued. Most importantly, the connection to these zero length files did not get closed and my session would quickly run out of FD.

I wonder if anyone has any idea how I can fix this.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Can all distributions in Stan be vectorized? Is vectorizing distributions improve speed?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Can all distributions in Stan be vectorized? Is vectorizing distributions improve speed?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jiang Du,

On Oct 19, 2015, at 11:27 PM, Jiang Du <jiang...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi, I'm a beginner of Stan, and I'm not that confident to vectorize all my distribution statements in Stan, for example, I know
>
> when mu is a vector, delta is a scalar,
> for(i in 1:N){
> y[n]~dnorm(mu,delta)
> }
>
> is the same as
>
> y~dnorm(mu, delta)
> , is the sense that delta is broadcasted to a vector with the same size as mu, or y, i.e., N.

I see you're coming from R. Stan uses "normal" instead of "dnorm."

> Can I do the same thing for all the distributions in Stan?
> For example,
> Vector[N] x;
> x~uniform(a,b) # a, b are both scalar
>
>
> matrix[K,K] sigma[N];
> sigma ~ inv_wishart(m, S) # S is a single matrix with the same dim as each element of sigma array, broadcast??
>

No, we don't have all the multivariate distributions vectorized. The way to determine if it is vectorized is to look at the function signature either in the manual or through rstan (I forget the function to look up Stan functions).

Plural arguments indicate that it can be given either a scalar or a vector type. For example, "reals" means that argument can accept a real, a row_vector, a vector, or a 1-d array of reals.

> Also, for increment_log_prob(), it can take a vector, suppose I have a vector of log_likelihood log_vec, which way is better:
> increment_log_prob(sum(log_vec))
> #or
> increment_log_prob(log_vec)
>

My guess is the second is better, but this won't impact the overall readability or runtime either way.

> Thanks for your patience and hope you don't mind if this question is too simple. I went over the menu 2 times but I'm still not feeling confident when writing programs.

messages.subject: Question about parallel evaluation
messages.body_plain:
hi

I am trying to understand how evaluating probability for a model like

   vector[t] x;
   for (t in 2:N)
     x[t] ~ normal(f(x[t-1]), sig);

might be evaluated in a multithreaded fashion. It seems that if you only
need the log probability, it's trivially parallelizable, the terms can
be evaluated independently and then summed.

However, Stan uses gradient, so derivative information has to be
propagated the loop in the above model.

In parallel computing projects, such a structure suggests a scan
algorithm, where the derivative could be propagated through a thread's
part of the model, and then afterwards combined.

Just to clarify, I don't mean to ask that Stan implement this, rather
I'm curious if this it possible to implement the log probability
gradient calculation in such a way.

Thanks!
Marmaduke

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Complex hierarchical model --- any hints?
messages.body_plain:
The cauchy's just a weakly informative prior --- if you have more info
about your distribution's tails, by all means use it!

The only place integers should matter in Stan is (1.0 / 3.0) vs. (1 / 3).

Chains typically get stuck in hierarchical models with wildly varying posterior
scales.  You can try reducing initial step size and increasing the
target acceptance rate, which will slow down the model but make it more
robust to getting stuck.

- Bob

> On Oct 19, 2015, at 7:41 PM, Jan Tünnermann <je...@mail.upb.de> wrote:
>
> Dear Andrew,
>
> thanks for the quick reply.
> On 10/20/2015 01:17 AM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
>> Hi, here are some quick thoughts:
>> 1.  We recommend putting the Stan program in a separate .stan file rather than encoding it as a character string.  That’ll be easier when you want to fit the model more than once.
> Great, I was already wondering how to make use of that feature (because I read people talking about fitting models without recompiling).
>> 2.  Hard constraints on parameters are typically a good idea.  Inherent constraints (such as sigma>0) are fine, but constraints such as <-.2,.2> are typically a badd idea.  Better to use a prior, for example replacing a hard <-.2,.2> constraint by a prior such as N(0,.1) or N(0,.2).
> OK, I'll try that. I must admit I was using the uniform ranges becaue I can imagine the range from which samples are drawn more intuitively.
>> 3.  Similarly for the parameter you bound between 0.01 and 0.99.  If it can’t be 0.995, it probably is highly unlikely to be 0.985.  Etc.
> That's true. The idea was to not put in any information (which I probalby still do) but avoid extreme values that may lead to problems in the functions ...
> These parameters are acutally biases between 0 and 1 that are neutral at 0.5. Is there any prior distribution favorable for such cases?
>> 4.  No need to write 0 and 8 as 0.0 and 8.0.
> I always do so if a language allows it. Can avoid hard-to-find erros is statically typed languages. Also helps me to keep track whether there is a continous range or discrete integer values.
>> 5.  The Cauchy priors could be a bit weak.  I suggest replacing by normal or something like t_3 or t_7 if you want some long tails.
> I think you may be right here. I have been following the advice from your (2003?) paper on priors for variance parameters.Hence the Cauchys. But I observed in the posteriors that the sigmas of many variables look rather normally distributed.
>
> The problem is, I have little feeling for how informative certain priors (or contraints) may be. For simpler models in JAGS I just had it generate prior predictive distirbutions by running the model without data. I'm not sure if that is an option here as well.
>
>> I suspect that none of these tips will solve your problem, but who knows?  Maybe!  I’m thinking it can’t hurt to put in some priors.
>
>> A
> Thanks again,
> Jan

Hi Bob,

On 10/20/2015 04:17 PM, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> The cauchy's just a weakly informative prior --- if you have more info

Do observations of serious trial and error runs count as information in
this case (say, I try a lot of different priors, but the posterior
always looks like a normal with roughly the same location and scale)? Or
do you mean theoretically justified knowledge?

>
> The only place integers should matter in Stan is (1.0 / 3.0) vs. (1 / 3).
>
> Chains typically get stuck in hierarchical models with wildly varying
> posterior
> scales.

I'm just trying something that may improve the model in this aspect.
Most parameters are in the roughly range between 0 and 1 in that model.
Two however are rather in the of 0 and 100. I try to bring the ranges
closer together by adding constant factors. I'm not sure though if that
is a good (or possible way)  ...

> You can try reducing initial step size and increasing the
> target acceptance rate, which will slow down the model but make it more
> robust to getting stuck.

I have not came across yet how to control these sampling parameters.
I'll look it up in the manual.

Jan

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Zero-Inflated Negative Binomial
messages.body_plain:
What's going on is that Stan's using a default step size to start,
and then uses the posterior gradient, which is only a linear approximation
to the curvature.  The problem is that it can cause us to step over a boundary.
Starting with smaller step sizes tends to help reduce these warnings at the
cost of more run time.

Michael's teaching us to be worried if there is even one such warning
(reported as divergent iterations --- the divergence is that there's not
a finite log density) in the sampling part of the run.

You usually don't want to recompute expressions.  So this:

>   for (n in 1:N) {
>     if (Y[n] == 0)
>       increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(bernoulli_logit_log(1,d0 + d1 * X[n,1]),
>                                       bernoulli_logit_log(0, d0 + d1 * X[n,1])
>                                       + neg_binomial_2_log_log(Y[n], b0 + b1 * X[n,2],phi)));
>     else
>       increment_log_prob(bernoulli_logit_log(0,d0 + d1 * X[n,1])
>                           + neg_binomial_2_log_log(Y[n], b0 + b1 * X[n,2], phi));

would be a bit more efficient as

>   for (n in 1:N) {

     real temp;
     temp <- d0 + d1 * X[n,1];

>     if (Y[n] == 0)

To follow up on Bob's comment about stepsize, since you're using RStan you can add the 'control' argument (a named list) to your call to the stan(). You can either directly manipulate stepsize using

control = list(stepsize = value)

or alternatively you can increase the target metropolis acceptance rate using

control = list(adapt_delta = value),

which will also lead to a smaller stepsize. The default for adapt_delta is 0.8, so you could try setting it to .9 or even higher and it should help avoid those warnings.

Jonah

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Complex hierarchical model --- any hints?
messages.body_plain:
Yes, fitting other models counts.  It doesn't match the
prescriptive theory of Bayes (choose a prior, observe some
data, update to posterior), but it matches the practice of
model criticism and updating.

If you have one parameter in (0,1) and another in (0,100)
range, you probably want to bring them both down into the (-1/2, 1/2)
range or (-1,1) scale.  (Not a hard constraint, just most of
the probability mass.)  But that'd require multiplying and
shifting.

The way to control those parameters varies in name by interface,
but the doc of what they do is in the Stan language manual in the
part on algorithms.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Zero-Inflated Negative Binomial
messages.body_plain:
And you can do both.  If you set the stepsize lower, it helps
during warmup not have errors and if you set target acceptance
higher, it makes things more stable.  Calling this a "Metropolis"
accept rate is misleading --- it's an average acceptance rate from
points on the HMC trajectory in NUTS's slice sampler.

- Bob

> On Oct 20, 2015, at 6:03 PM, Jonah Sol Gabry <jga...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> To follow up on Bob's comment about stepsize, since you're using RStan you can add the 'control' argument (a named list) to your call to the stan(). You can either directly manipulate stepsize using
>
> control = list(stepsize = value)
>
> or alternatively you can increase the target metropolis acceptance rate using
>
> control = list(adapt_delta = value),
>
> which will also lead to a smaller stepsize. The default for adapt_delta is 0.8, so you could try setting it to .9 or even higher and it should help avoid those warnings.
>
> Jonah
>
> On Tuesday, October 20, 2015, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> What's going on is that Stan's using a default step size to start,
> and then uses the posterior gradient, which is only a linear approximation
> to the curvature.  The problem is that it can cause us to step over a boundary.
> Starting with smaller step sizes tends to help reduce these warnings at the
> cost of more run time.
>
> Michael's teaching us to be worried if there is even one such warning
> (reported as divergent iterations --- the divergence is that there's not
> a finite log density) in the sampling part of the run.
>
> You usually don't want to recompute expressions.  So this:
>
> >   for (n in 1:N) {
> >     if (Y[n] == 0)
> >       increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(bernoulli_logit_log(1,d0 + d1 * X[n,1]),
> >                                       bernoulli_logit_log(0, d0 + d1 * X[n,1])
> >                                       + neg_binomial_2_log_log(Y[n], b0 + b1 * X[n,2],phi)));
> >     else
> >       increment_log_prob(bernoulli_logit_log(0,d0 + d1 * X[n,1])
> >                           + neg_binomial_2_log_log(Y[n], b0 + b1 * X[n,2], phi));
>
> would be a bit more efficient as
>
> >   for (n in 1:N) {
>      real temp;
>      temp <- d0 + d1 * X[n,1];
> >     if (Y[n] == 0)
> >       increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(bernoulli_logit_log(1, temp),
> >                                       bernoulli_logit_log(0, temp)
> >                                       + neg_binomial_2_log_log(Y[n], b0 + b1 * X[n,2],phi)));
> >     else
> >       increment_log_prob(bernoulli_logit_log(0, temp)
> >                           + neg_binomial_2_log_log(Y[n], b0 + b1 * X[n,2], phi));
>
>
> but probably wouldn't be noticeable.  You could make it even faster by defining
> a vector on the outside and access it as:
>
>   {
>      vector[N] temp;
>      temp <- d0 + d1 * col(X, 1);
>
>      ... replace temp above with temp[n] ...
>
> Same for b0 and b1.  And it's more efficient if you declare X as an
> array of vectors, so that the equivalent of col() is constant time.
>
> - Bob
>
> On Oct 20, 2015, at 4:04 PM, Jonah <jga...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Hi Kenneth, that message you're seeing is more of a warning than an error, and you'll often get a few of these during warmup when you have parameters with constraints. But that's ok. As long as you're not getting a ton of them after the warmup period and you're getting good results (e.g. recovering the parameters from the fake data simulation, etc.) then you're fine.
> >
> > Jonah
> >
> > On Tuesday, October 20, 2015 at 2:53:26 PM UTC-4, Kenneth Lowande wrote:
> > Hi Jonah,
> >
> > Thanks for the helpful reply. It runs and seems to perform well. However, I still get errors like the following.
> >
> >
> >
> > I've noticed similar errors in other GLMs - even when they appear to be working correctly. Any idea what may be causing this?
> >
> > Revised model code below:
> >
> > model_code <- '
> >
> > data {
> >   int<lower=1> N;
> >   int<lower=1> K;
> >   real X[N,K];
> >   int<lower=0> Y[N];
> > }
> >
> > parameters {
> >   real<lower=0> phi;
> >   real b0;
> >   real b1;
> >   real d0;
> >   real d1;
> > }
> >
> >
> > model {
> >   #priors:
> >   phi ~ normal(0,5);
> >   b0 ~ normal(0,5);
> >   b1 ~ normal(0,5);
> >   d0 ~ normal(0,5);
> >   d1 ~ normal(0,5);
> >
> >   #data model:
> >   for (n in 1:N) {
> >     if (Y[n] == 0)
> >       increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(bernoulli_logit_log(1,d0 + d1 * X[n,1]),
> >                                       bernoulli_logit_log(0, d0 + d1 * X[n,1])
> >                                       + neg_binomial_2_log_log(Y[n], b0 + b1 * X[n,2],phi)));
> >     else
> >       increment_log_prob(bernoulli_logit_log(0,d0 + d1 * X[n,1])
> >                           + neg_binomial_2_log_log(Y[n], b0 + b1 * X[n,2], phi));
> >
> >   }
> >  }
> > '
> >
> >
> > On Monday, October 19, 2015 at 5:14:57 PM UTC-4, Jonah wrote:
> > Also, if you do end making theta a linear predictor then you can use bernoulli_logit_log instead of bernoulli_log because theta will then be on the logit scale. If you use bernoulli_log you'll need to compute inv_logit(theta) whereas bernoulli_logit_log will do that for you and will be more computationally stable.
> >
> > On Monday, October 19, 2015 at 5:12:28 PM UTC-4, Jonah wrote:
> > Hi Kenneth,
> >
> > A few tips:
> >
> > 1) You want to use neg_binomial_2_log_log instead of neg_binomial_2_log. The names are unfortunate, but the former allows you to keep your linear predictor on the log scale. We really need to change the names because neg_binomial_2_log does seem like what you want but you need the extra _log at the end.
> >
> > 2) In your simulations you say that z is the logit regressor but in your model both x and z are used in the negative binomial rather than the bernoulli. Typically you'd use the same predictors (x in this case) in both calls to the negative binomial distribution and use z in a model for the bernoulli parameter theta. To do this, theta doesn't need to be declared as a parameter (just d0 and d1) and then you can construct theta in the model block, since it would be a deterministic function of d0, d1 and the data z. On a related note, I noticed that that the d0 and d1 parameters don't factor into your simulations of the data. I would generate z from a normal distribution and then compute inv_logit(d0 + d1 * z) and use that as the probabilities for the bernoulli in your simulations instead of just taking z from a uniform(0,1).
> >
> > 3) For both theoretical and computational reasons we recommend much tighter priors than normal(0,500), which gives non-negligible weight to values like -1000 and 1000. For your example you probably don't need anything wider than normal(0, 5), and you could probably even go tighter than that.
> >
> > Hope that helps,

That's a hard constraint governed by mathematical requirements of
positive definiteness.  So you need to declare

  real<lower=0, upper=max_rho> rho;

to make sure rho in (0, max_rho).  It will get an implicit uniform
distribution on the valid values, so you don't need to include the uniform
distribution.

> > If the median of the posterior is around 0.17, you shouldn't set
> > the max  at 0.173 ---- it will be problematic with the transform
> > we use to be that close to the boundary and may be causing the

messages.body_plain:
The problem is that those non-converging chains may be indicating
that there's something biased in the sample you do get.  When they
get stuck, it's usually because the sampler fell into a tightly
constrained neck of a funnel somewhere --- if you don't explore
the necks of the funnels, you get biased estimates.  But if you
try to explore them with too-large step sizes, the sampler virtually
hangs, never being able to find the escape direction.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
RStan's set up to parallelize by default as of 2.8.0.

I believe 1 or 0.1 is the default, so 0.01 is a small-ish initial
step size.  It's all problem dependent.  We set things up assuming
all parameters were roughly normal(0, 1) distributed.

You can also look at where you're having problems in ShinyStan
(or even in some of the RStan output, I believe).  If you're getting
stuck way out in the tail, then you might be able to initialize in
a more reasonable place and avoid the problem. But if you're getting
stuck in a volume of high posterior mass, then you might need
to reparameterize into a more favorable posterior geometry.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Multilevel beta-binomial
messages.body_plain:
Sorry --- we're getting bogged down with all the people sending us
long and involved models these days.  So posts that don't lead
with a specific question tend to get ignored.

I'll give your questions a shot.

1.  Yes, it's kosher to transform the variables you sample.  That's
just a new random variable defined as a function of the old ones and
the posterior's legit.  You should do this in Stan's generated quantities
so you can monitor convergence.

2.  Didn't get the context about comparing.  But in general, you want
to do a posterior event probability along the lines of Pr[theta[1] > theta[2]].
In Stan, that just means assigning an int value to 1 if the property holds
and 0 otherwise and looking at the posterior mean.

3.  Beta-binomial is a distribution that marginalizes the binomial parameter
out of a compound beta-binomial:

  p(y,  theta | a, b) = beta(theta | a, b) * binomial(y | N, theta)

and then marginalizing out theta to get

  BetaBinom(y | a, b)

  = INTEGRAL_0^1 beta(theta | a, b) * binomial(y | N, theta) d.theta

- Bob

> On Oct 16, 2015, at 7:37 PM, Mike Boedigheimer <mbo...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>
> Hi
>
> I hope this is an ok forum to get feedback on a model I'm working on. The model is included below and it seems to work and compile. But I'm new to heirarchical modeling, and I'd like to get feed back on whether this is reasonable or whether there is a different approach that you'd recommend instead. I'll give a bit of background
>
> I have dataset where we count the total number a certain kind of cell in a specimen (n) and then count a specific sub-type within that total (x). I consider x as a binomial random variable with an unknown proportion, theta. We take these measurements on groups of individuals that have been randomized to one of several treatment groups at baseline prior to treatment and over time after treatment. We also have historical data on the proportion of these cell types over time within and between untreated subjects.
> The STAN model is shown below. theta is true, unknown mean proportion in the untreated population. tau_b is a precision parameter governing the between subject variability around theta. It is gamma distributed and we usually have some information on this -- i.e. not intended to be non-informative. theta_j is the unknown true mean for the jth subject.  At time i, the true sample level mean for subject j will be theta_ij and it fluctuates around theta_j according to a beta distribution with precision parameter tau_w. tau_w is also given an informative or weakly informative gamma prior. Theta_ij is also influence by a set of fixed parameters that I want to make inference on. Specifically, is there a treatment effect (at any dose level) on the proportion of this sub-type of cell.
>
> Some features of the model that I think I like, are that the baseline samples do not have special importance. They are simply a realization of a beta distributed variable like every other time point. Also, the treatment effect happens at the subject level, theta_j, rather than the global mean, theta. The result is a larger effect for subjects with proportions near 50%, which does seem to capture some aspects of the data we observe.
> I have not applied this prospectively on real data. On data that I've simulated (which complies completely with my assumed distributions -- not realistic), the model seems to work far better than previous linear baseline adjusted models of log transformed data, which I have tried. In fact it works so well, that I suspect I'm not making correct inference here.
>
> Say X is the design matrix built based on post dose visits including an interaction between dose and visit. Dose groups are reference encoded (placebo = 0s), so other parameters are relative to that. Visits are encoded so they sum to 0 (i.e. the last visit is the -sum(other visits). So for two dose groups and three visits the design matrix is:
>
> Visit  Dose  col1(visit), col2(dose), col3(interaction)
> V2     D0      1               0                  0
> V2     D1      1               1                  1
> V3     D0     -1               0                  0
> V3     D1     -1               1                 -1
> PRE  any     0               0                  0
>
> I calculate posterior group means from a linear combination of the sampled u's and theta's. inv_logit( L*u + logit(theta) ) and make inferences based on credible intervals. I have also examined the same linear combinations of u to make inference.
>
> Few specific questions:
> 	• Is this legit?
> 	• How can I ask whether any of the treated groups differ from placebo (comparing lp__ from a model without u?)?
> 	• I've seen beta-binomial before, but the examples were too simple. Is my model still considered a beta-binomial, or is it beta-beta-beta-binomial??
>
> Sorry this was so long. Thanks for any input.
>
>
>
>
> model {
>    vector[N] theta_i;
>
>    theta ~ beta(theta_0[1],theta_0[2]);
>    tau_b ~ gamma(gamma_b[1], 1/gamma_b[2] );
>
>
>    tau_w  ~ gamma( gamma_w[1], 1/gamma_w[2] );
>    theta_j ~ beta( tau_b*theta, tau_b*(1-theta) );
>
>
>    u ~ normal( u_0, se_0 );         // prior for "fixed" coefficients
>
>    for (i in 1:N) {
>         theta_i[i] <- inv_logit( X[i]*u + logit(theta_j[grp_i[i]]) );
>         }
>
>
>     theta_ij ~ beta( theta_i*tau_w, (1-theta_i)*tau_w );
>     x ~ binomial( n,theta_ij );
>
>
>  }
>
>
>

messages.body_plain:
This is exactly how I finally understood them (thanks, Michael!)

I completely agree that simulations really help.  Both ways.
Simulate x ~ uniform(0,1), plot x and note it's uniform, plot
logit(x) and note it's not.  In fact, it's the logistic, because
the logit function is the inverse CDF for the logistic distribution
(that makes inverse logit the CDF).  You can do the same thing
with the Phi() function (inverse unit normal CDF) and the normal.

I really like Krzysztof's example of the Stan program that samples
from a different density without the Jacobian adjustment.  We're
also doing that in some of our education examples --- trying to
show what happens when things go wrong, how to diagnose it, and how
to debug the model and fix the problem.

- Bob

> On Oct 21, 2015, at 9:39 AM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> The problem with Jacobians is that to really motivate them you have to
> get into the non-uniqueness of densities, i.e. there is some abstract
> probabilistic system that we can represent with infinitely many
> parameterizations.  Samples are not dependent on such a density,
> however, just the abstract probabilistic system, so they must remain
> invariant.
>
> One thing to do would be to take a density, p(theta), and some transform,
> f(theta), and compare
>
> 1. Samples drawn from p(theta) then mapped by f, f_{i} = f(theta_{i})
> 2. Samples drawn from p(f(theta)).
>
> They should not be the same, as easily established by comparing
> histograms of the samples, or a histogram of (1) compared to the
> density p(f(theta)).  Then to the proper transform,
>
> p(f(theta)) df/dtheta,
>
> and show that they are the same.
>
> I’m not sure if there’s anything more intuitive, as you’re always
> working with two spaces (the original and the transformed) and
> there’s always going to be confusion between the two.
>
>
> On Oct 20, 2015, at 9:43 PM, Krzysztof Sakrejda <krzysztof...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>> I recently did a brief intro to Stan and I tried to come up with an example of
>> a model that needs a Jacobian adjustment due to a transformation and can
>> be explained in fairly intuitive terms.  The density I used was one with a normally
>> distributed radius parameter and a uniformly distributed angle parameter.  The first
>> Stan model was:
>>
>> data {
>>   real r_mu;
>>   real r_sd;
>> }
>>
>> parameters {
>>   real x;
>>   real y;
>> }
>>
>> model {
>>   real r;
>>   r <- sqrt(x^2+y^2);
>>   r ~ normal(r_mu, r_sd);
>> }
>>
>> This version of the model, when looking at the samples of r_mu, estimates something like
>> 8.5 instead of the 8 used to simulate the data.  With the Jacobian adjustment the model was:
>>
>> model {
>>   real r;
>>   matrix[2,2] J;
>>   real lad_J;
>>   r <- sqrt(x^2+y^2);
>>   r ~ normal(r_mu, r_sd);
>>
>>   # Sigh, this model needs more maths:
>>   J[1,1] <- x/sqrt(x^2+y^2);
>>   J[1,2] <- y/sqrt(x^2+y^2);
>>   J[2,1] <- (x^2*(x^2+y^2)^(-3.0/2.0) - (x^2+y^2)^(-1.0/2.0)) / sqrt(1-(x^2)/(x^2+y^2));
>>   J[2,2] <- (x*y) / ((x^2+y^2)^(3.0/2.0) * sqrt(1-(x^2)/(x^2+y^2)));
>>   lad_J <- log(fabs(J[1,1]*J[2,2] - J[1,2]*J[2,1]));
>>   increment_log_prob(lad_J);
>> }
>>
>> This nails the r_mu (and the difference between the two is clearly visible with something like 4k samples of r_mu).  It's sort of intuitive that without the adjustment the sampler would spend too much time on the outer ring and too little on the inner ring leading to an over-estimate for r
>>
>> I guess the "log(x) ~ normal()" example might be simpler in some ways, but this one had the benefit of forcing me to figure out which derivatives go where.
>>

messages.body_plain:
Hi Shuaiqi,

Thanks for sending the code. I haven't been able to replicate the problem you mentioned, so I'm not sure what happened when you were getting those errors. The model as you have it now seems to work ok, but not great. In particular the Rhats and effective sample sizes for lp__ and sigma_epsilon are a bit concerning.

Instead of epsilon ~ normal(0, sigma_epsilon), I would suggest defining the epsilon vector in transformed parameters as the product sigma_epsilon * epsilon_raw, where epsilon_raw is declared in the parameters block, is the same size as epsilon, and is given standard normal priors (i.e. epsilon_raw ~ normal(0,1)). Statistically this is the same thing as what you currently have but it should help with sampling and I think you'll see the problematic Rhats decrease and effective sample sizes increase.

Jonah

Re: [stan-users] Compound Poisson-Gamma model for zero-inflated continuous data
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Compound Poisson-Gamma model for zero-inflated continuous data
messages.body_plain:
This

> int ngis[n_obs];

declares a local variable which is never defined before it used
here:

>     ngis[s] ~ poisson(lambda[s])T[1,];

Stan doesn't work this way --- the ~ doesn't do a random number
generation.  Nor does it define a graphical model the way BUGS does.
It just increments the log density with the value of the probability
function at the argument.  If the arguments are undefined, so is the
result.

One thing Stan can't do is latent Poisson variables.  So if everything
hinges on that, then you won't be able to use Stan.  Usually these
models go the other way around, though, with a continuous mixture.

So it looks like the Tweedie distribution is going to be beyond
Stan's ability to model as is;  here's what the Wikipedia says:

  In probability and statistics, the Tweedie distributions are a family of probability
  distributions which include the purely continuous normal and gamma distributions,
  the purely discrete scaled Poisson distribution, and the class of mixed compound
  Poisson–gamma distributions which have positive mass at zero, but are otherwise continuous.

The only way it'd be possible is if ngis could be analytically marginalized out.

- Bob

> On Oct 21, 2015, at 8:24 PM, Miguel de Val-Borro <miguel...@gmail.com> wrote:

?  x is both the outcome and the mean ?  That's the same as 0 ~ normal(0, errx).

> but this fails because x is a matrix. The only way I cae n get this to work is to slice
> the array using the row function.
>
>                 for (i in 1:k) row(x, i) ~ normal(row(x, i), row(errx, i));

> there is any other way to define this model?

There's also something wrong in the above in that you let i run from 1:k,
but the matrix is (n x k), so it has n rows, not k rows.

There's a chapter in the manual on arrays vs. matrices with efficiency
concerns.  For this, you can do something like this:

  to_vector(x) ~ normal(to_vector(y???), to_vector(err_x))

which will flatten things out.   Instead of row(x, i), you can use x[i], but it's
even better then to make x an array of vectors --- no copying that way.

We haven't yet implemented vectorization that takes parallel matrices.

- Bob

Yes, sometimes the stable parameters are slower than the
ones that don't work.  Failing can be fast.  Or it can be
slow --- depends on whether the step size vanishes to zero
(slow failure) or you get arithmetic errors (fast failure).

See the CmdStan manual chapter on data input format for
a full definition with examples.

It's an ASCII format (downsides: slow to decode, bloated;
upsides: easy to produce, portable).

The .R extension is just what R uses for R code and
the data input format we use is a subset of R code.

messages.subject: Conceptual question about time-varying parameter models
messages.subject_clean: Conceptual question about time-varying parameter models
messages.body_plain:
All -

I'm trying to reconcile the performance difference of two models. The first model is estimated on some (extending) window of data, at the end of which it produces a 1-year ahead forecast. For example, it estimates up to the end of 1975 then produces a forecast for 1976; the window then extends to include 1976, the model is re-fitted, and I generate a forecast for 1977. As the window size is increased, I get a series of true out-of-sample forecasts.

The second model is a time-varying parameter model estimated over the full data set. In each period within the sample, I generate a 1-year ahead forecast using that period's parameters. So the parameters for 1975 are used to forecast for 1976, and those for 1976 are used to forecast 1977.

The second model performs much better than the first, which is not surprising. My question is whether this is a valid comparison; in a time-varying-parameter model with a parameter theta[t] ~ normal(theta[t-1], sigma), are the values of theta[t-1] influenced at all by the data that come after? Another way of putting it is if i were to estimate the model to the end of 1975, would I have the same 1975 parameters in expectation as the case of estimating the model to today?

Cheers,
Jim

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] A potential scalability issue in my model
messages.body_plain:
Thanks.  That helps.  But it's still even easier if you
just give us the whole program in one big block.  It's hard
for a second person to come in and piece it all back together.
But I think I see what you're doing now.

> Given my model: y = X * beta + u + e,  I wrote: y ~ normal(mu + u, b); why is this not appropriate?

Yes, that's appropriate.  I was just lost in the types.  I now see
you're multiplying L by a vector to get a vector u.

I think you should probably declare L as

  cholesky_factor_cov[N] L;

That will makes sure that L really is a Cholesky factor for
a positive-definite matrix.  And it'll make the intent of your
program easier for others to follow.

Or you could take in the covariance matrix and do the cholesky
factoring in the transformed data block.  It only gets run once
as the data is read in.

I still don't understand why you'd want to add a scale term.
Isn't the covariance matrix already scaled?  What we often do
is work in terms of a scaled correlation matrix.

In general, multiplying two parameters can be problematic
because it introduces a multiplicative non-identifiability, which
even with priors, tends to lead to a banana-shaped posterior.
This is bad news because the posterior covariance then isn't
position independent, and therefore Stan's HMC algorithms can't
find good global step sizes and mass matrices for jumping --- they
just have to take something very small, which is costly in log
density evaluations.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Conceptual question about time-varying parameter models
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Conceptual question about time-varying parameter models
messages.body_plain:
I’m not sure what you mean by that.  Either you have parameters
that are constant in time or parameters that vary in time.  If a
parameter varies in time (really you have a different parameter
for each time point) then future values can certainly improve the
inference of past values (think smoothing in a Kalman filter).
Now you can use those improved inferences to simulate forecasts
but you have to be careful with the interpretation — it’s a valid
posterior predictive check _on the complete time series that was
measured_ but not a valid measure of predictive performance on
entirely new data.

On Oct 23, 2015, at 12:06 AM, James Savage <jav...@gmail.com> wrote:

> I'm modelling the parameters as adjusting due to a random walk (although ex-post they look stationary). So to my mind that would invalidate the comparison?
>
> On Friday, October 23, 2015 at 9:29:59 AM UTC+11, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> > It depends on the details of the model.  For example, if the parameters you’re
> > estimating are stationary then it’s valid to use the fit from the full data to inform
> > the 1-year forecast simulations.  This would be true for the parameters in
> > AR, MA, ARMA, etc processes, but not the states themselves.
> >
> > On Oct 22, 2015, at 11:24 PM, James Savage <jav...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > > All -
> > >
> > > I'm trying to reconcile the performance difference of two models. The first model is estimated on some (extending) window of data, at the end of which it produces a 1-year ahead forecast. For example, it estimates up to the end of 1975 then produces a forecast for 1976; the window then extends to include 1976, the model is re-fitted, and I generate a forecast for 1977. As the window size is increased, I get a series of true out-of-sample forecasts.
> > >
> > > The second model is a time-varying parameter model estimated over the full data set. In each period within the sample, I generate a 1-year ahead forecast using that period's parameters. So the parameters for 1975 are used to forecast for 1976, and those for 1976 are used to forecast 1977.
> > >
> > > The second model performs much better than the first, which is not surprising. My question is whether this is a valid comparison; in a time-varying-parameter model with a parameter theta[t] ~ normal(theta[t-1], sigma), are the values of theta[t-1] influenced at all by the data that come after? Another way of putting it is if i were to estimate the model to the end of 1975, would I have the same 1975 parameters in expectation as the case of estimating the model to today?

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] non-matching arrays are not fatal?
messages.body_plain:
I agree that should be the behavior.  Daniel --- is there an
issue to add this behavior for indexing errors?  I know we've
talked about it.

What's going on now is that all of our error-checking
conditions throw the same type of domain error for illegal
inputs.

What will happen in the future is that we'll separate causes
for errors, like index mismatches, which are not recoverable
in normal programs and things like hitting 0 bounds, which may
not be a problem in future iterations (the "divergences" in Michael's
and now Stan's terminology).

Now consider this fiendish program

  parameters {
    real<lower=0, upper=1> theta;
    ...

  model {
    if (theta < 0.5)
      y[20] ~ normal(mu, sigma);
   else
      y[10] ~ normal(mu, sigma);

Now if 20 is out of range and 10 is in range, and theta is
unconstrained, the program will fail for proposals of theta < 0.5
and succeed for proposals of theta > 0.5.

So the change will slightly break backward behavior, but we
decided that's a good thing here because we haven't been able
to imagine a situation where the above was intentional.  We don't
want ways to add back-door rejection because it breaks the derivatives
underlying all of our algorithms.

- Bob

the idea of change of variables and the definition of Jacobian
adjustments in 2D finally led me to understanding
the purpose of a determinant.  Same way that understanding
covariance led me to understand positive definiteness
and the multivariate normal let me understand
rotation, scaling and eigendecomposition.  In fact, it might
be fun to write an intro to these topics based on the univariate
and multivariate normal.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Intuitive example of Jacobian adjustment
messages.body_plain:
2D would be fine it done carefully.  For example, consider f: x \mapsto x^{3},
with a Gaussian density pi(x) and an integral \int_{A} pi(x)dx.

You start with drawing a grid to represent dx, a gradient showing pi(x)
and a line circumscribing the region of integration A (make it a circle
for simplicity).  You can then add samples drawn from a proper Markov
chain and compare the MCMC estimate to the true integral.

Then apply the map. First you’ll see the grid change and the density warp.
Then when you integrate over f(A) you should get a different value.  Draw
samples and see that they don’t one up with f( old samples).

Finally add the Jacobian to the density, which yields the right integral and
proper samples that line up with f(old samples).

I thought there is an open issue, but couldn't find it easily.

> On Oct 23, 2015, at 12:05 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
> I agree that should be the behavior.  Daniel --- is there an
> issue to add this behavior for indexing errors?  I know we've
> talked about it.
>
> What's going on now is that all of our error-checking
> conditions throw the same type of domain error for illegal
> inputs.

We actually changed that behavior. We now throw different errors. I'm not sure it is the correct error for every use, but it should be close.

>
> What will happen in the future is that we'll separate causes
> for errors, like index mismatches, which are not recoverable
> in normal programs and things like hitting 0 bounds, which may
> not be a problem in future iterations (the "divergences" in Michael's
> and now Stan's terminology).
>
> Now consider this fiendish program
>
>  parameters {
>    real<lower=0, upper=1> theta;
>    ...
>
>  model {
>    if (theta < 0.5)
>      y[20] ~ normal(mu, sigma);
>   else
>      y[10] ~ normal(mu, sigma);
>
> Now if 20 is out of range and 10 is in range, and theta is
> unconstrained, the program will fail for proposals of theta < 0.5
> and succeed for proposals of theta > 0.5.
>
> So the change will slightly break backward behavior, but we
> decided that's a good thing here because we haven't been able
> to imagine a situation where the above was intentional.  We don't
> want ways to add back-door rejection because it breaks the derivatives
> underlying all of our algorithms.

Yes, it breaks backwards compatibility, but I think that's relying on behavior that wasn't quite in our spec.

If anyone finds the issue, can you post it here or bump it up on the issue tracker?

Daniel

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Intuitive example of Jacobian adjustment
messages.body_plain:
This is so going in the book!  Or the manual or wiki.  Or
all of those good things we have left to do.

- Bob

> On Oct 23, 2015, at 12:28 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> 2D would be fine it done carefully.  For example, consider f: x \mapsto x^{3},
> with a Gaussian density pi(x) and an integral \int_{A} pi(x)dx.
>
> You start with drawing a grid to represent dx, a gradient showing pi(x)
> and a line circumscribing the region of integration A (make it a circle
> for simplicity).  You can then add samples drawn from a proper Markov
> chain and compare the MCMC estimate to the true integral.
>
> Then apply the map. First you’ll see the grid change and the density warp.
> Then when you integrate over f(A) you should get a different value.  Draw
> samples and see that they don’t one up with f( old samples).
>
> Finally add the Jacobian to the density, which yields the right integral and
> proper samples that line up with f(old samples).
>
>
> On Oct 23, 2015, at 5:15 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
>> For me, I understood the 1D case, and then understanding
>> the idea of change of variables and the definition of Jacobian
>> adjustments in 2D finally led me to understanding
>> the purpose of a determinant.  Same way that understanding
>> covariance led me to understand positive definiteness
>> and the multivariate normal let me understand
>> rotation, scaling and eigendecomposition.  In fact, it might
>> be fun to write an intro to these topics based on the univariate
>> and multivariate normal.
>>
>> - Bob
>>
>>> On Oct 23, 2015, at 12:09 PM, Krzysztof Sakrejda <krzysztof...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>>
>>> On Wednesday, October 21, 2015 at 1:42:42 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>>> This is exactly how I finally understood them (thanks, Michael!)
>>>
>>> I completely agree that simulations really help.  Both ways.
>>> Simulate x ~ uniform(0,1), plot x and note it's uniform, plot
>>> logit(x) and note it's not.  In fact, it's the logistic, because
>>> the logit function is the inverse CDF for the logistic distribution
>>> (that makes inverse logit the CDF).  You can do the same thing
>>> with the Phi() function (inverse unit normal CDF) and the normal.
>>>
>>> Yeah, the 1-D examples are probably easier to explain although the
>>> 2-D is helpful since it makes the issue of geometry into one of
>>> change-of-area which I think can be more intuitive so likely both.
>>>
>>>
>>> I really like Krzysztof's example of the Stan program that samples
>>> from a different density without the Jacobian adjustment.  We're
>>> also doing that in some of our education examples --- trying to
>>> show what happens when things go wrong, how to diagnose it, and how
>>> to debug the model and fix the problem.
>>>
>>> I attached the full models and code to run them in case you're interested in the example.
>>> This was rushed so I hard-coded some directories... sorry!
>>>
>>> Krzysztof
>>>
>>>
>>>
>>>
>>>
>>>
>>>
>>> - Bob
>>>
>>>> On Oct 21, 2015, at 9:39 AM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>>>
>>>> The problem with Jacobians is that to really motivate them you have to
>>>> get into the non-uniqueness of densities, i.e. there is some abstract
>>>> probabilistic system that we can represent with infinitely many
>>>> parameterizations.  Samples are not dependent on such a density,
>>>> however, just the abstract probabilistic system, so they must remain
>>>> invariant.
>>>>
>>>> One thing to do would be to take a density, p(theta), and some transform,
>>>> f(theta), and compare
>>>>
>>>> 1. Samples drawn from p(theta) then mapped by f, f_{i} = f(theta_{i})
>>>> 2. Samples drawn from p(f(theta)).
>>>>
>>>> They should not be the same, as easily established by comparing
>>>> histograms of the samples, or a histogram of (1) compared to the
>>>> density p(f(theta)).  Then to the proper transform,
>>>>
>>>> p(f(theta)) df/dtheta,
>>>>
>>>> and show that they are the same.
>>>>
>>>> I’m not sure if there’s anything more intuitive, as you’re always
>>>> working with two spaces (the original and the transformed) and
>>>> there’s always going to be confusion between the two.
>>>>
>>>>
>>>> On Oct 20, 2015, at 9:43 PM, Krzysztof Sakrejda <krzysztof...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>>>
>>>>> I recently did a brief intro to Stan and I tried to come up with an example of
>>>>> a model that needs a Jacobian adjustment due to a transformation and can
>>>>> be explained in fairly intuitive terms.  The density I used was one with a normally
>>>>> distributed radius parameter and a uniformly distributed angle parameter.  The first
>>>>> Stan model was:
>>>>>
>>>>> data {
>>>>> real r_mu;
>>>>> real r_sd;
>>>>> }
>>>>>
>>>>> parameters {
>>>>> real x;
>>>>> real y;
>>>>> }
>>>>>
>>>>> model {
>>>>> real r;
>>>>> r <- sqrt(x^2+y^2);
>>>>> r ~ normal(r_mu, r_sd);
>>>>> }
>>>>>
>>>>> This version of the model, when looking at the samples of r_mu, estimates something like
>>>>> 8.5 instead of the 8 used to simulate the data.  With the Jacobian adjustment the model was:
>>>>>
>>>>> model {
>>>>> real r;
>>>>> matrix[2,2] J;
>>>>> real lad_J;
>>>>> r <- sqrt(x^2+y^2);
>>>>> r ~ normal(r_mu, r_sd);
>>>>>
>>>>> # Sigh, this model needs more maths:
>>>>> J[1,1] <- x/sqrt(x^2+y^2);
>>>>> J[1,2] <- y/sqrt(x^2+y^2);
>>>>> J[2,1] <- (x^2*(x^2+y^2)^(-3.0/2.0) - (x^2+y^2)^(-1.0/2.0)) / sqrt(1-(x^2)/(x^2+y^2));
>>>>> J[2,2] <- (x*y) / ((x^2+y^2)^(3.0/2.0) * sqrt(1-(x^2)/(x^2+y^2)));
>>>>> lad_J <- log(fabs(J[1,1]*J[2,2] - J[1,2]*J[2,1]));
>>>>> increment_log_prob(lad_J);
>>>>> }
>>>>>
>>>>> This nails the r_mu (and the difference between the two is clearly visible with something like 4k samples of r_mu).  It's sort of intuitive that without the adjustment the sampler would spend too much time on the outer ring and too little on the inner ring leading to an over-estimate for r
>>>>>
>>>>> I guess the "log(x) ~ normal()" example might be simpler in some ways, but this one had the benefit of forcing me to figure out which derivatives go where.
>>>>>
>>>>> Do you have a favorite model for explaining the whole Jacobian adjustment thing?
>>>>>

>
> > Given my model: y = X * beta + u + e,  I wrote: y ~ normal(mu + u, b); why is this not appropriate?
>
> Yes, that's appropriate.  I was just lost in the types.  I now see
> you're multiplying L by a vector to get a vector u.
>
> I think you should probably declare L as
>
>   cholesky_factor_cov[N] L;

    Will do this.

>
> That will makes sure that L really is a Cholesky factor for
> a positive-definite matrix.  And it'll make the intent of your
> program easier for others to follow.
>
> Or you could take in the covariance matrix and do the cholesky
> factoring in the transformed data block.  It only gets run once
> as the data is read in.
>
> I still don't understand why you'd want to add a scale term.
> Isn't the covariance matrix already scaled?  What we often do
> is work in terms of a scaled correlation matrix.

    The covariance matrix was already scaled. The intention to put the scale factor was to scale the actual values of the random variables u, while u ~ L * z. While cov(u) ~ L, I thought there might be an additional scale on u for its real effect on the response, just like the parameter of another fixed predictor.

    Almost certain this is unnecessary, because the estimation of z will automatically give u in the right scale, given y. Please let me know if I miss anything.

>
> In general, multiplying two parameters can be problematic
> because it introduces a multiplicative non-identifiability, which
> even with priors, tends to lead to a banana-shaped posterior.
> This is bad news because the posterior covariance then isn't
> position independent, and therefore Stan's HMC algorithms can't
> find good global step sizes and mass matrices for jumping --- they
> just have to take something very small, which is costly in log
> density evaluations.
>
> - Bob

> >
> > - Bob

> > > On Oct 22, 2015, at 2:23 PM, Xulong Wang <emai...@gmail.com> wrote:

On Friday, October 23, 2015 at 3:37:27 PM UTC-4, Miguel de Val-Borro wrote:
> I wanted to make separate packages for Stan C++, pystan, rstan etc so that
> all the interfaces depend on Stan C++ and is not installed independently.
> I am not sure if this could work because I am not familiar with the source.

This could work, but it is a lot of effort just to conserve disk space. I started to write a script to do this for linux servers a few months ago and then lost it when my battery died. It went something like this:
Do a git clone of CmdStan and make sure to pull in the Stan Math Library git submodule
Set environmental variables for STAN_HOME and CMDSTAN_HOME
Download JuliaStan, MatlabStan, and perhaps StataStan. Those all just call CmdStan but need to have environmental variables to tell them where to look.
In R, do install.packages("StanHeaders") and then go into the directory where the StanHeaders package is installed and replace the include/stan directory with a symlink to ${CMDSTAN_HOME}/stan/lib/stan_math/stan and replace the include/src directory with a symlink to ${CMDSTAN_HOME}/stan/src.
In R, do install.packages("rstan")
That would probably get you 90 percent of the way there, but there are probably some things I am forgetting. PyStan seems to insist on copying everything it needs to a build directory, so I'm not sure if you could get it to work off of the submodules of CmdStan.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Hierarchical negative binomial model
messages.body_plain:
May I ask what you read before you tried to write this
model?  The reason I ask is that the two problems in your
code are quite common and we'd like to be able to more
clearly formulate the issues.

Issue 1.

The variables in Stan need to be declared with constraints
so that any value satisfying the constraints has finite
log density.  So when you have a parameter declared
as

>   real sigma;

and a sampling statement

>   sigma ~ uniform(0,10);

you produce a problem where sigma < 0 or sigma > 10 satsify
the declared constraints (there aren't any).

If you insist on this prior, you need to declare

  real<lower=0, upper=10> sigma;

and similarly for the other parameters.

Issue 2.

You are using the local variable seed2 before it is defined:

  int seed2[N];
  ...

    seed2[i] ~ neg_binomial_2(lamda[i], phisd);

Stan doesn't work like BUGS --- this just increments the posterior
log density.  In BUGS, it defines an edge in a directed graphical
model.

I think the only solution is to marginalize seed2 out of your
model.  I'm not sure how a compound negative binomial works.  You're
giving your model a double-dose of overdispersion.

Issue 3.

You can't raise an array to a power, so seed2^beta is going to
be ill-formed as well.  The legal signatures are defined in the
index to the manual.

- Bob

On Sunday, October 25, 2015 at 8:58:08 PM UTC-4, Satwik Acharyya wrote:
> How large ??  In my case the count is 8 when i am running 100 simulations.

8% is not great. You may be able to get rid of them with a higher degrees of freedom parameter for the inverse Wishart but we don't recommend using the inverse Wishart distribution in the first place. It is generally much better to parameterize a covariance matrix into the product a diagonal matrix of standard deviations, a correlation matrix,  and the diagonal matrix of standard deviations again. In that case, you can put some reasonable prior on the standard deviations and an lkj_corr(1) prior on the correlation matrix (or even better an lkj_cholesky_corr(1) prior on its Cholesky factor). There are many examples of this reparameterization in the manual and on the Stan-users list.

Ben

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] What happens before the first sample?
messages.body_plain:
It can do up to 100 initializations before giving up when
it can't find an initialization that works.  So the first
iteration can do 100 evaluations of the log density and
gradient even if it doesn't go anywhere.  Of course, it might
do 1000 evaluations in one iteration under default parameters, too --- depends on the
model and inits.   So you should see how many leapfrog steps
were done in that step.

Also, make sure that every value of variables that satisfies
the declared constraints has finite log density in the model.
If not, init has to do a lot of guessing and then sampling can
devolve to a random walk because of boundary rejections.

- Bob

messages.subject: Maximum likelihood and random effects; problem.
messages.subject_clean: Maximum likelihood and random effects; problem.
messages.body_plain:
I am helping teach a course in hierarchical models, and want to show the students (a plurality of whom are grad students in education) how to use Stan from R. They've already learned how to use lme4, and so they're familiar with MLE procedures. I wanted to start by using Stan for MLE-like estimation, so they could treat the outcome as they're used to with an MLE. In other words, to use the "optimizing" command and invert the Hessian, rather than doing MCMC.

So, I went off and started to build some of the simple hierarchical models we've worked with, in Stan. And at first, it seemed to work; the estimates were close enough to the comparable ones from lmer, that I could chalk up any small differences to the effects of the priors I was using. (We're teaching them to use either minimally-informative priors like inv_gamma(.001,.001), for consistency with what they've done before; or, better, to use weakly-informative priors like T₃.)

But when the data set was a little bit smaller, there was sometimes a problem: Stan would want to set the variance of the random effects to zero. For a while, I couldn't figure it out. After all, wasn't this just MLE; and if there was a problem with Stan, shouldn't there be a similar problem with lmer?

Then I realized: lmer's MLE maximizes the likelihood conditional on the parameters, and only fits the random effects once it's done so; but Stan is effectively maximizing the likelihood conditional on the parameters and the random effects. So setting variance for the random effects arbitrarily close to 0 means arbitrarily high likelihood.

(Note: I know there's standard terminology for the almost-a-likelihood that I'm maximizing here, but I can't recall it at the moment. Can somebody tell me the right words?)

So, as I see it, here are my options for avoiding this problem (though some are probably impractical):
1. Just give up and use MCMC. The problem comes from using a Bayesian tool for frequentist procedures; the fix is to not do that. However, this means giving the students more theory and practical tricks than I want to; and it's also a lot slower than maximization.
2. Use variational methods (ADVI). Since these fit a seperable approximation of the full posterior, I can easily integrate out over the random effects, and find the maximum of the thing I want. Unfortunately, this is not yet possible with rstan.
3. Try to correct for this. Basically, if I could integrate over the random effects, that would be like subtracting the log of the precision with which I know them, which is proportional to the Fisher information conditional on both the data and the parameters which I'm maximizing but using expectation over the random effects. Assuming rough normality, the precision with which I know each random effect is basically a sum of the precision from the next level up — the inverse variance of the hyperdistribution — and the precision from the next level down — in the simplest case, the inverse variance of the residuals, divided by the number of observations in the relevant group. So, roughly speaking, I could adjust the log likelihood by adding log(sigma_alpha+sigma_y/harmonic_mean(n_j)), where each n_j is the size for group j.
4. Ignore the problem. Put a prior on the log of the random effect variance that's strong enough to keep it from slamming into zero, and live with the fact that it's downwardly biased and not as good as the number I'd get from lmer.

I'm leaning towards option 3, and being a bit fast and loose with the math (as you can already see from my suggestion of using harmonic means). But I'd like advice from the list. Is my understanding of the problem reasonable? Are the solutions I've enumerated better or worse than I think they are, in terms of either feasibility or effectiveness? Are there other ways to deal with this? What key words do I need to search for find the literature on this kind of issue?

Thanks a lot,
Jameson

>  (We're teaching them to use either minimally-informative priors like inv_gamma(.001,.001), for consistency with what they've done before; or, better, to use weakly-informative priors like T₃.)

Andrew is having a strong influence — I’m starting to get chills every time I see inv_gamma(.001,.001) priors...

> (Note: I know there's standard terminology for the almost-a-likelihood that I'm maximizing here, but I can't recall it at the moment. Can somebody tell me the right words?)

Maximum marginal likelihood.

> 1. Just give up and use MCMC. The problem comes from using a Bayesian tool for frequentist procedures; the fix is to not do that. However, this means giving the students more theory and practical tricks than I want to; and it's also a lot slower than maximization.

Not really — optimization in Stan yields a perfectly fine frequentist ML estimator.  It’s more that the asymptotics
necessary to motivate said estimator are not valid for hierarchical models.

> 2. Use variational methods (ADVI). Since these fit a seperable approximation of the full posterior, I can easily integrate out over the random effects, and find the maximum of the thing I want. Unfortunately, this is not yet possible with rstan.

This would give you something of a weird estimator — in particular I have no idea how you’d analyze its sampling
distribution.

> 3. Try to correct for this. Basically, if I could integrate over the random effects, that would be like subtracting the log of the precision with which I know them, which is proportional to the Fisher information conditional on both the data and the parameters which I'm maximizing but using expectation over the random effects. Assuming rough normality, the precision with which I know each random effect is basically a sum of the precision from the next level up — the inverse variance of the hyperdistribution — and the precision from the next level down — in the simplest case, the inverse variance of the residuals, divided by the number of observations in the relevant group. So, roughly speaking, I could adjust the log likelihood by adding log(sigma_alpha+sigma_y/harmonic_mean(n_j)), where each n_j is the size for group j.

Lots of assumptions in there which can lead to odd behaviors in the estimators.  At the very least it will require
lots of empirical investigation to understand the ultimate performance.

> 4. Ignore the problem. Put a prior on the log of the random effect variance that's strong enough to keep it from slamming into zero, and live with the fact that it's downwardly biased and not as good as the number I'd get from lmer.

I believe this is the best option until you can (approximately or numerically) marginalize out the random effects.
