Dear Stan (rstan) user,

I am trying to estimate a stereotype logit model using rstan, but run into problems. I would appreciate it if anyone could point me to the right direction. I would be more than happy to share the codes once I work it out. Following are two documents that discuss this model. Basically it is a reduced rank multinomial logit model, with the slopes varying across equations by a set of scalar factors that are constrained between 0 and 1 (corner constraints) to retain ordinality and obtain identification.

http://psfaculty.ucdavis.edu/bsjjones/stereotypelogit.pdf

http://deepblue.lib.umich.edu/bitstream/handle/2027.42/64310/3693_ftp.pdf?sequence=1
(see page 3149 for how some of the key parameters are given priors using Dirichlet distribution)

Jun Xu, PhD
Associate Professor
Department of Sociology
Ball State University

Here are some excerpts of the error/warning messages that I got from running the following codes:
Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:
Invalid value of phi: validate transformed params(N4stan5agrad3varE): phi[4] is -0.211538:0, but must be greater than or equal to 0
If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,
but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified.
Rejecting proposed initial value with zero density.

Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:
Invalid value of phi: validate transformed params(N4stan5agrad3varE)error occurred during calling the sampler; sampling not done
> print(stanFit)
Stan model 'modelString' does not contain samples.

Below are my r codes (see the attached files for the r script and data)
Codes
###

rm(list=ls(all=TRUE))
require(rstan)
require(MASS)
require(VGAM)
require(foreign)

mydta <- read.dta("gssCum7212Teach.dta", convert.factor=F)

usevar <- c("health", "age", "educ", "impinc", "female", "year")
mydta <- mydta[complete.cases(mydta[usevar]),]

usedta <- subset(mydta, select=c(health, age, educ, impinc, female))

# set seed to get the same random sample each time
set.seed(47306)
usedta <- usedta[sample(1:nrow(usedta), size = 1000, replace=T),]

# here is the DATA used for estimation
save(usedta, file = "stanData.RData")

myologit <- polr(as.ordered(usedta$health) ~ usedta$age + usedta$educ + usedta$impinc +usedta$female,
                 method = c("logistic"))
summary(myologit)

# stereotype logit model
stereotypeLogitR1 <- rrvglm(as.factor(health) ~ age + educ + impinc + female,
                            multinomial,
                            usedta)
summary(stereotypeLogitR1)
# slotNames(stereotypeLogitR1)

#------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# THE MODEL.

modelString = "
data {
    int<lower=2> M; // number of response levels
    int<lower=1> N; // number of observations
    int<lower=1> K; // number of predictors
    int<lower=1, upper=M> y[N]; // y variables
    row_vector[K] x[N]; // x vectors
    vector<lower=0>[M-1] alpha;
}

parameters {
    vector[K] b;
    vector[M-1] theta;
    vector[M-1] gamma;
}

transformed parameters{
    vector<lower=0, upper=1>[M] phi;
    phi[1] <- 0;
    phi[2] <- gamma[1];
    phi[3] <- gamma[1] + gamma[2];
    phi[4] <- gamma[1] + gamma[2] + gamma[3];
}

model {
    vector[M] prob;
    vector[M] emu;

    // specify priors
    for (m in 1:M-1)
        gamma ~ dirichlet(alpha);
    for (k in 1:K)
        b[k] ~ normal(0, 100);
    for (m  in 1:M-1)
        theta[m] ~ normal(0, 100);
    for (n in 1:N) {
            emu[1] <- exp(phi[1]*x[n]*b);
            for (m in 2:M)
                emu[m] <- exp(theta[m] + phi[m]*x[n]*b);
            for (m in 1:M)
                prob[m] <- emu[m]/sum(emu);
            y[n] ~ categorical(prob);
    }
}

# generated quantitaties {
#
# }

" # close quote for modelstring

# translate model to C++ and compile to DSO:
stanDSO <- stan_model(model_code=modelString)

# prepare data
dataMat = as.matrix(usedta)

# Rename for use by generic processing later:
nData = NROW(dataMat)
x = dataMat[,-1]
predictorNames = colnames(dataMat)[-1]
nPredictors = NCOL(x)
y = as.matrix(dataMat[,1])
predictedName = colnames(dataMat)[1]
nYlevels = max(y)
distAlpha = rep(1,3)

dataList = list(
    x = x ,
    y = as.vector( y ) , # BUGS does not treat 1-column mat as vector
    K = nPredictors ,
    N = nData ,
    M = nYlevels,
    alpha = distAlpha
)

# get initial values for b
bInit = - coefficients(stereotypeLogitR1)[-c(1:3)]
thetaInit = - coefficients(stereotypeLogitR1)[c(1:3)]

initsList =  list(
    b = bInit,
    theta = thetaInit)

# specify parameter values for MCMC sampling
parameters = c("b", "theta", "gamma")  # The parameter(s) to be monitored.
adaptSteps = 1000              # Number of steps to "tune" the samplers.
burnInSteps = 1000            # Number of steps to "burn-in" the samplers.
nChains = 3
seedNum = 60115
# Number of chains to run.
initsChains <- list()
# initials for three chains
for (i in 1:nChains) {
    initsChains[[i]] <- initsList
}
#}
numSavedSteps=10000           # Total number of steps in chains to save.
thinSteps=1                   # Number of steps to "thin" (1=keep every step).
nPerChain = ceiling( ( numSavedSteps * thinSteps ) / nChains ) # Steps per chain.

# Sampling MCMC chain
cat( "Sampling final MCMC chain...\n" )

# monitor time
time.used <- proc.time()

stanFit <- sampling(object=stanDSO,
                data=dataList,
                seed = seedNum,
                pars=parameters,
                chains=nChains,
                thin=thinSteps,
                  # init=initsChains
                iter=nPerChain,
                warmup=burnInSteps )
print(stanFit)

May I also ask you what you read of the Stan doc before
trying this?  We need to somehow get the message about
satisfying constraints across, because most of the questions
we're getting lately are from people who didn't realize
that all parameters must be constrained so that any values
satisfying the constraints has a positive (non-zero) density (or
finite log density).

I don't have time to read about a new model, but the
issue you're getting from Stan is exactly what it says it
is.  You assigned phi to a value that does not satisfy
its declared constraints.  The source of this problem is here:

> parameters {
>     vector[K] b;
>     vector[M-1] theta;
>     vector[M-1] gamma;
> }
>
> transformed parameters{
>     vector<lower=0, upper=1>[M] phi;
>     phi[1] <- 0;
>     phi[2] <- gamma[1];
>     phi[3] <- gamma[1] + gamma[2];
>     phi[4] <- gamma[1] + gamma[2] + gamma[3];
> }

Because gamma is unconstrained, it's valid for it to have values like -1
or 127, neither of which are going to allow phi to satisfy
that lower=0, upper = 1 constraint.  Maybe you want to inv-logit transform
those gammas as is typical in ordered logit models?

Alternative, you can define

  real<lower=0, upper=1> gamma1;
  real<lower=0, upper= 1 - gamma1> gamma2;
  real<lower=0, upper = 1 - gamma2> gamma3;

We have built-in operations to do a lot of the things you're
implementing from scratch, like softmax.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Maximum likelihood and random effects; problem.
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Maximum likelihood and random effects; problem.
messages.body_plain:
> On Oct 27, 2015, at 7:55 AM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>> (We're teaching them to use either minimally-informative priors like inv_gamma(.001,.001), for consistency with what they've done before; or, better, to use weakly-informative priors like T₃.)
>
> Andrew is having a strong influence — I’m starting to get chills every time I see inv_gamma(.001,.001) priors...

Check out the advice in our manual and in the papers of Andrew's
we've cited.  Those inv_gamma(0.001, 0.001), contrary to popular belief,
have a huge impact on posteriors because of how they concentrate prior
mass.

>
>> (Note: I know there's standard terminology for the almost-a-likelihood that I'm maximizing here, but I can't recall it at the moment. Can somebody tell me the right words?)
>
> Maximum marginal likelihood.

AKA "empirical Bayes", but we also discourage that term because
it's no more empirical than full Bayes --- it's just a biased
approximation (the bias is underestimating lower level parameter
posterior variance and arises from treating the hierarchical parameters
as having a point estimate).

>> 1. Just give up and use MCMC. The problem comes from using a Bayesian tool for frequentist procedures; the fix is to not do that. However, this means giving the students more theory and practical tricks than I want to; and it's also a lot slower than maximization.
>
> Not really — optimization in Stan yields a perfectly fine frequentist ML estimator.  It’s more that the asymptotics
> necessary to motivate said estimator are not valid for hierarchical models.
>
>> 2. Use variational methods (ADVI). Since these fit a seperable approximation of the full posterior, I can easily integrate out over the random effects, and find the maximum of the thing I want. Unfortunately, this is not yet possible with rstan.
>
> This would give you something of a weird estimator — in particular I have no idea how you’d analyze its sampling
> distribution.
>
>> 3. Try to correct for this. Basically, if I could integrate over the random effects, that would be like subtracting the log of the precision with which I know them, which is proportional to the Fisher information conditional on both the data and the parameters which I'm maximizing but using expectation over the random effects. Assuming rough normality, the precision with which I know each random effect is basically a sum of the precision from the next level up — the inverse variance of the hyperdistribution — and the precision from the next level down — in the simplest case, the inverse variance of the residuals, divided by the number of observations in the relevant group. So, roughly speaking, I could adjust the log likelihood by adding log(sigma_alpha+sigma_y/harmonic_mean(n_j)), where each n_j is the size for group j.
>
> Lots of assumptions in there which can lead to odd behaviors in the estimators.  At the very least it will require
> lots of empirical investigation to understand the ultimate performance.
>
>> 4. Ignore the problem. Put a prior on the log of the random effect variance that's strong enough to keep it from slamming into zero, and live with the fact that it's downwardly biased and not as good as the number I'd get from lmer.
>
> I believe this is the best option until you can (approximately or numerically) marginalize out the random effects.

Vince Dorie (with Andrew and others) have a paper on which priors you can use
to avoid boundaries in MLE.

- Bob

We tried to emphasize the way that sampling statements
work.  Anyway, not a big deal as we're planning to drop
the "~" notation anyway because it's just confusing our
users who assume on seeing it that it either (a) works
like BUGS to define a graphical model, or (b) actually
performs a draw as in a forward simulation.  It's just
shorthand for incrementing the log density.

The key point is that every set of values that satisfies
the constraints must be in support.  If you do

  vector<lower=0,upper=1>[K] gamma;

then gamma[1] = gamma[2] = ... = gamma[K] = 0.99 satisfies
the variable's constraint, but is not in support for a Dirichlet.

But then you don't want to have that 0 you had distributed
by dirichlet(alpha) anyway --- it's out of support if you look
at the definition.

If you really just need a simplex, do this:

data {
  vector<lower=0>[K] alpha;
  ...
parameters {
  simplex[K] gamma;
  ...
model {
  gamma ~ dirichlet(alpha);
  ...

- Bob

It's configurable.  See the algorithms part of the manual.

And the number of draws you need depends on how easy the posterior
geometry is to move around.  If you have a very simple theta ~ normal(0, 1);
model then the initial state's going to be very good as a starting point
and it won't take long at all to adapt.

always run everything in something like Hadoop which would check
jobs being up and help combine the results if you want to
encapsulate all the back and forth.

- Bob

messages.subject: A question on convergence
messages.body_plain:
Hi

I looked and I haven't seen the following result mentioned anywhere> I know you put up with a lot and I apologize if it is trodden ground. Two questions below will be is the result known? Is it something to worry about?

I have fit a model with around 100 parameters on 8 threads with 1000 simulations per thread. Other than threads, I'm using all default parameters. R hat is 1 for all of the parameters and mixing looks good. No problems there.

The interesting part is if someone were to show me a "new" posterior draw from a one of these threads, I would be to predict which thread it came from with 60% accuracy (uniform positive predictive value across thread). That is pretty good compared to a random guess of 12.5%. I base this claim on 10-fold cross-validation using a quadratic discriminant classifier using the 100 parameters as predictors for the threads.  KNN also performs well.

The result persists using 1000 to 2000 or 4000 warmups.

The result does not seem to be specific to any one dataset. But, it could be model specific. I've only tested one model which is an hierarchical binomial with random beta variables for within and between subject variability. I posted that model on an earlier post.

This result seems to imply that the samplers in each thread are exploring different parts of the posterior or are dwelling too long on particular spots.

Honestly, the posterior means don't seem to change too much due to this, but they seem to change a little. If I compare the posterior means from one of these threads to  a "true" mean estimated from very sparse sampling.

Thanks for all your help.

messages.body_plain:
That's expected for MCMC --- the draws in each Markov chain
are correlated.  That's why the effective sample size
is less than the sample size.

If the 10-fold x-validation used a random subset of
points in each chain rather than removing a contiguous
10% subset, I wouldn't be surprised if the accuracy was
even higher from classification.  I'd also guess that accuracy
goes down as the chains get longer.  Imagine Metropolis
here --- you get rejections and then have copies of
exactly the same point in a chain.  The probability of
that same duplication in another chain is measure 0.

- Bob

Are you using RStan?  If so I use the function

# Count divergences across all chains
count_divergences <- function(fit) {
  sampler_params <- get_sampler_params(fit, inc_warmup=FALSE)
  sum(sapply(sampler_params, function(x) c(x[,'n_divergent__']))[,1])
}

Divergences are really sensitive diagnostics to
problems that could be causing stray chains.

conditional distribution and doesn’t tell you anything about the joint distribution
that we actually care about.

probably your best bet is to suck it up and look at the samples plotting vs
_every_ pair of parameters.  It helps to highlight the ones that ended with
a divergence in a different color than the others.  You want to look for
“banana" shapes or really any sharp corner that indicates nonlinear
nonidentifiabilities that are preventing efficient sampling or “funnel” shapes
that indicate bad hierarchical structure.

result!

will converge slower than functions that very weakly.  For example, constants
have no variation and converge immediately.  The log posterior density tends to
vary strongly and hence converge more slowly.

numerical estimates) are good.  Given what you’re seeing in the chains, they’re
probably not.

messages.subject: Unused parameters
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

this maybe a stupid question, but I have been wondering about the following.

Imagine I have some unused parameters, that is, they are defined but not
connected to any model structure. Do these possibly effect the sampling
of a model in the following situations:

a) There is only the definition (no constraints)
b) There is a definition with upper and lower bounds
c) There is a sampling statement and case (a)
d) There is a sampling statement and case (b)

Intuitively I think case (a) and (b) should not do any harm except some
runtime required for initializing and drawing uniform samples. For case
(c) it still might be just some runtime increase. Case (d) might be more
critical, because the sampling statement may generate to-be-rejected
samples.  Furthermore, maybe the adaptation process may be affected by
the pure existence of such dangling parameters?

Many thanks in advance!
Jan

messages.body_plain:
The point is that you need a properly normalizable
posterior for Stan to work at all.  As long as the
posterior's proper, it should only cause inefficiency,
not failure.

If the model doesn't touch the variable, then the
posterior is equal to the prior.

Stan's default prior is uniform over values meeting
the constraints.

So unconstrained, or just constrained above or below
are improper, constrained above and below are proper.
Simplexes and correlation matrices are proper, ordered
vectors and covariance matrices are improper.

You don't need sampling statements, per se, you can use
increment_log_prob.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Bob, I believe your predictions are true. I.e. if I train on the 1st half of each chain and predict the second half, I don' t get strong predictions (sometimes anti-predictive). It is also true that longer chains are slightly weaker. Although it is still easily detectable up to 40,000 total simulations. Also, if I thin the data by 1/8 the predictive value is not detectable. So I have to agree that correlation is a culprit.

I will add one more thought by suggesting PCA might be a more sensitive way to detect this. I still find non-random latent variables in the PCA analysis after thinning the data by 1/40 or more.

I am concluding that thinning is still best practice for HMC (even though I read many times that thinning should not be necessary with HMC). It may not matter much, or at all, for inference on a single parameter, but it looks like it might when making inference on linear combinations of the parameters (as I am in this problem). If you disagree please let me know.

As always I want to thank you for your and the teams dedicated work on STAN and this forum.

> I am concluding that thinning is still best practice for HMC (even though I read many times that thinning should not be necessary with HMC). It may not matter much, or at all, for inference on a single parameter, but it looks like it might when making inference on linear combinations of the parameters (as I am in this problem). If you disagree please let me know.

Thinning is not good for substantive inference because the draws contain some information even if they are not quite independent within chain. Your example seemed to mix really well though, so there was not very much within-chain dependence at all. Once in a great while (with NUTS) thinning is a necessary evil to work around hardware limitations. But the best thing to do is make the linear combination of stuff in generated quantities so that you can verify its MCMC standard error is acceptably small to make inferences with.

Ben

Andy

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: A question on convergence
messages.body_plain:
Ok. I thought I was good, and now I'm confused. Are you saying that it is worse to thin 1e6 draws by drawing every 1/1000 samples than it is to accept chains with known dependence from 1000 draws?  how about 1 sample each from 1e3 chains? My intuition is way off here, so if you can point me to some reference materials that speak to this I'd really appreciate it.

Even if I generate the linear combinations as quantities within STAN, I'm not sure I'm safe to trust MC standard error. If the draws are correlated it cannot be safe unless the chains are long enough that that the tails of all the interesting quantities are evenly sampled!

So, for now, I've updated my my position to think I may not have sampled enough so that the linear combinations of interest are evenly sampled. I will base my assessment on whether the PCA analysis reveals NO latent variables among the normalized parameters. I will see whether I can investigate what happens if I run 1000 threads with 1e9 samples each. Let me know if you think this is interesting or a (predictable) waste of time (and what the outcome will be;). Will the PCA analysis converge to 0 latent variables?

Best regards

MIke

If you disagree please let me know.

Your example seemed to mix really well though, so there was not very much within-chain dependence at all. Once in a great while (with NUTS) thinning is a necessary evil to work around hardware limitations. But the best thing to do is make the linear combination of stuff in generated quantities so that you can verify its MCMC standard error is acceptably small to make inferences with.
>
> Ben

messages.body_plain:
Hi Andy,

I don't know of a generic function, but it is easy to write one
(horribly non generic):

lll2array <- function(lll) {
  l <- length(lll)
  m <- length(lll[[1]])
  n <- length(lll[[1]][[1]])
  a <- array(0,c(l,m,n))
  for (i in 1:l) {
    l2 <- lll[[i]]
    stopifnot(length(l2) == m)
    for (j in 1:m) {
      l3 <- l2[[j]]
      stopifnot(length(l3) == n)
      a[i,j,] <- as.vector(l3,"numeric")
    }
  }
  a
}

## test it
test_lll <- local({
  test1 <- list(1,2)
  test2 <- list(test1,test1,test1)
  list(test2,test2,test2,test2)
})
test_lll                                # nasty
lll2array(test_lll)                     # nice

That said, possibly building up your data as an array in the first place
could be a better choice.

Best,

Tamas

data {

moment.

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I've found that for the rewritten model described in my previous post, which is linear in f and where f has true value 1, changing the bounds on the uniform prior seems to affect the adaptation of the NUTS. With my initial prior which was uniform on the interval (0,1.2) I found that, while most chains converge to the true value of f quickly, for chains with an initial parameter value >1.1 they seem to take a much longer time, drifting downwards towards the true value. If you run the NUTS for enough iterations (here 100,000) eventually all the chains make a 'jump' near to the true value, from where they then converge rapidly. The attached file lin_longrun_0_1pt2.png are the traceplots for this.

But if I widen my prior so that it is uniform on the interval (0,2) I find that all of the chains rapidly converge. There is none of this slow adaptation period in a certain part of the parameter space. lin_longrun_0_2.png is the corresponding traceplot for this prior. The same behaviour holds when I use a uniform prior on the interval (0.8,1.2) as demonstrated by the traceplot, lin_longrun_0pt8_1pt2.png. But again a slight change in the prior so that it is no longer centred on the true value of f, so making it uniform on the interval (0.8,1.4) say (traces plotted in lin_longrun_0pt8_1pt4.png) sees some of the chains which start near to 0.8 take much longer to converge to the true value, when there were no issues in this region of the parameter space with the previous prior. Starting a chain with an initial f value of 0.806 with this slightly expanded prior, and with the seed in stan set to 120591, it takes around 5000 iterations of the NUTS before there is a jump near to the true value. With the prior which is symmetric about the true value however (uniform between 0.8 and 1.2) this initial value and seed sees an almost immediate convergence to the true value.

Bob mentioned in his post how stan likes parameters on a unit scale and how this can affect adaptation and suggested several alterations, and I am wondering what affect my choice of the bounds of my uniform prior are having on the adaptation of the NUTS.

Thanks,
Michael

On Thursday, October 29, 2015 at 9:00:19 AM UTC-4, Mike Boedigheimer wrote:
> Actually, in this case already I already have 100% efficiency (8000 Reff/8000 samples) for most parameters, Rhat is 1 and there is excellent mixing on a univariate level. I'm talking about eliminating any correlations by thinning after the simulation is done to remove thread-specific multi-parameter co-variance or means

Thinning is not going to help. When the output comes up and says that you have this or that ESS for a parameter, it indicates that the average of all the somewhat dependent draws has the same precision as you would expect from a simple random sample from the posterior distribution of size ESS. If you were to throw away some of your draws and then take an average, its precision would be no higher than the precision you would expect from a simple random sample from the posterior distribution of size ESS. It is similar to if you had a sample of data that were generated by an AR(1) process and you wanted to estimate the mean of the process, you would use the whole sample rather than some fraction of it.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am running the following on two different computers, which have different c++ compilers, and I seem to be getting different results:

fit <- stan(file = aStanModel, data = data, iter = 1000, chains = 1, seed=1)

One computer is a Mac which produces the following under gcc --version:

Configured with: --prefix=/Applications/Xcode.app/Contents/Developer/usr --with-gxx-include-dir=/usr/include/c++/4.2.1

Apple LLVM version 5.1 (clang-503.0.38) (based on LLVM 3.4svn)

Target: x86_64-apple-darwin13.4.0

Thread model: posix

The other is a linux machine using:

gcc (GCC) 4.4.7 20120313 (Red Hat 4.4.7-11)

The fit object that is returned in both cases is different - samples, Rhats etc.

Does anyone know what might be causing this difference?

Best,

Ben

> Hi,

> I am running the following on two different computers, which have different c++ compilers, and I seem to be getting different results:

>
> Configured with: --prefix=/Applications/Xcode.app/Contents/Developer/usr --with-gxx-include-dir=/usr/include/c++/4.2.1
>
> Apple LLVM version 5.1 (clang-503.0.38) (based on LLVM 3.4svn)
>

>
> Thread model: posix
>
>
> The other is a linux machine using:
>
>
> gcc (GCC) 4.4.7 20120313 (Red Hat 4.4.7-11)

> The fit object that is returned in both cases is different - samples, Rhats etc.
>
>
> Does anyone know what might be causing this difference?

Yes. It's the compiler and the architecture.

Stan will reproduce the exact same draws with a fixed seed when the compiled target is the same. This requires:
- same architecture
- same compiler
- same compiler options, especially the optimization level
- same seed

Different compilers might do different things. Even with the "same" compiler (based on version number) across different architectures may produce different results. And we've definitely seen the same compiler, same seed, different optimization levels producing different results.

In your case, there's no reason to believe that you'll reproduce the same thing across different OSs and compilers.

> Best,

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for sharing.

Yes, it helps to rescale all the predictors so that
the coefficients are roughly unit scale.  Otherwise, Stan needs
to learn those scales during warmup.

What matters is the posterior, which you can think of as
the combination of prior knowledge plus data.  With little
data, you need more prior, as in hierarchical models or
something more constrained on an ordinary prior.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Stan with small fixed standard deviation
messages.body_plain:
See my comment to this post:

http://andrewgelman.com/2015/10/13/what-do-you-learn-from-p-05-this-example-from-carl-morris-will-blow-your-mind/

What matters is the posterior geometry --- the combination of
prior and data.  Changing an interval constraint can do major
things to the prior as shown above.  Even if it seems innocuous.

This is just one of the many reasons why we don't like interval
priors other than for parameters constrained to an interval (e.g.,
binomial chance of success parameters or correlation parameters).

- Bob

> On Oct 29, 2015, at 6:09 AM, Michael Thomson <michaelj...@btinternet.com> wrote:
>
> Hi,
>
> I've found that for the rewritten model described in my previous post, which is linear in f and where f has true value 1, changing the bounds on the uniform prior seems to affect the adaptation of the NUTS. With my initial prior which was uniform on the interval (0,1.2) I found that, while most chains converge to the true value of f quickly, for chains with an initial parameter value >1.1 they seem to take a much longer time, drifting downwards towards the true value. If you run the NUTS for enough iterations (here 100,000) eventually all the chains make a 'jump' near to the true value, from where they then converge rapidly. The attached file lin_longrun_0_1pt2.png are the traceplots for this.
>
> But if I widen my prior so that it is uniform on the interval (0,2) I find that all of the chains rapidly converge. There is none of this slow adaptation period in a certain part of the parameter space. lin_longrun_0_2.png is the corresponding traceplot for this prior. The same behaviour holds when I use a uniform prior on the interval (0.8,1.2) as demonstrated by the traceplot, lin_longrun_0pt8_1pt2.png. But again a slight change in the prior so that it is no longer centred on the true value of f, so making it uniform on the interval (0.8,1.4) say (traces plotted in lin_longrun_0pt8_1pt4.png) sees some of the chains which start near to 0.8 take much longer to converge to the true value, when there were no issues in this region of the parameter space with the previous prior. Starting a chain with an initial f value of 0.806 with this slightly expanded prior, and with the seed in stan set to 120591, it takes around 5000 iterations of the NUTS before there is a jump near to the true value. With the prior which is symmetric about the true value however (uniform between 0.8 and 1.2) this initial value and seed sees an almost immediate convergence to the true value.
>
> Bob mentioned in his post how stan likes parameters on a unit scale and how this can affect adaptation and suggested several alterations, and I am wondering what affect my choice of the bounds of my uniform prior are having on the adaptation of the NUTS.

messages.body_plain:
It means 23 times you ran into arithmetic troubles due to
underflow, overflow, divide by zero, subtracting two infinite
values, etc.  You really want that number to be zero.

You can try running with a higher target acceptance rate and
perhaps smaller initial step size.  Youc ould start with

  control = list(stepsize=0.01, adapt_delta=0.95)

and keep lowering.  By reducing the step size (and targeting
higher accept stat does that post warmup), the first-order
approximation of curvature via stepping according to the gradient
is more stable.

Each of those divergences should print a warning.  If you're
not seeing those, you should be.  And if you can't figure out
how to see them (I don't know RStan well enough to tell you), please
ask a separate question on the list so people will see it's new
and what the subject is.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
> On Oct 29, 2015, at 2:20 PM, Ben Lambert <ben.c....@googlemail.com> wrote:
>
> Ok, that explains some of the differences in diagnostics that I am achieving from using 1 chain vs 16. Up until now, was using just 1, but wanted to ramp up the number of iterations, so moved to 16 (being run in parallel).
>
> Before I was getting Rhat, NDivergent, etc. all looking fine, but when I move to many chains this isn't the case. Does this imply that previously chains were getting stuck in an area of the parameter space?

Yes.  If each of the chains for a parameter
converges to the same mean and sd, our n_eff
estimate reduces to doing them independently across
chains and adding them together.  Otherwise, it's
conservative as we believe it should be to reflect
that the chains aren't mixing well, so the means
and variances shouldn't be trusted.

There are complete definitions in the manual in
the chapter on MCMC.

- Bob

The rstan 2.8.x package will throw a warning if there are any divergent transitions after warmup that says:

"There were 23 divergent transitions after warmup. Increasing adapt_delta may help."

It will then make another warning suggesting that you use the pairs() function. So, looking at the output of get_sampler_params() should only be necessary if you need to know whether a particular chain is misbehaving.

messages.subject: Don't use hard constraints in priors unless you really have hard constraints
messages.subject_clean: Don't use hard constraints in priors unless you really have hard constraints
messages.body_plain:
Uniform priors are generally a bad idea unless the bounds represent true constraints (such as scale parameters being restricted to be positive).
I just now added this advice to the wiki on priors.
A

> On Oct 29, 2015, at 6:09 AM, Michael Thomson <michaelj...@btinternet.com> wrote:
>

> Hi,
>
> I've found that for the rewritten model described in my previous post, which is linear in f and where f has true value 1, changing the bounds on the uniform prior seems to affect the adaptation of the NUTS. With my initial prior which was uniform on the interval (0,1.2) I found that, while most chains converge to the true value of f quickly, for chains with an initial parameter value >1.1 they seem to take a much longer time, drifting downwards towards the true value. If you run the NUTS for enough iterations (here 100,000) eventually all the chains make a 'jump' near to the true value, from where they then converge rapidly. The attached file lin_longrun_0_1pt2.png are the traceplots for this.
>
> But if I widen my prior so that it is uniform on the interval (0,2) I find that all of the chains rapidly converge. There is none of this slow adaptation period in a certain part of the parameter space. lin_longrun_0_2.png is the corresponding traceplot for this prior. The same behaviour holds when I use a uniform prior on the interval (0.8,1.2) as demonstrated by the traceplot, lin_longrun_0pt8_1pt2.png. But again a slight change in the prior so that it is no longer centred on the true value of f, so making it uniform on the interval (0.8,1.4) say (traces plotted in lin_longrun_0pt8_1pt4.png) sees some of the chains which start near to 0.8 take much longer to converge to the true value, when there were no issues in this region of the parameter space with the previous prior. Starting a chain with an initial f value of 0.806 with this slightly expanded prior, and with the seed in stan set to 120591, it takes around 5000 iterations of the NUTS before there is a jump near to the true value. With the prior which is symmetric about the true value however (uniform between 0.8 and 1.2) this initial value and seed sees an almost immediate convergence to the true value.
>
> Bob mentioned in his post how stan likes parameters on a unit scale and how this can affect adaptation and suggested several alterations, and I am wondering what affect my choice of the bounds of my uniform prior are having on the adaptation of the NUTS.
>
> Thanks,
> Michael

>
> On Wednesday, October 28, 2015 at 9:42:53 PM UTC-7, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> > 1.  If your sampler is moving so slowly that you would be throwing away 99.9% of your draws, you have problems.  It’s possible for this to be ok, but usually when we do HMC and it’s working, the efficiency is much higher than 1/1000.
> >
> > 2.  The effective sample size takes into account correlation of the draws.  You can use the effective sample size from Stan, it is not necessary for draws to be independent.
> >
> > > On Oct 29, 2015, at 12:35 AM, Mike Boedigheimer <mbo...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > Ok. I thought I was good, and now I'm confused. Are you saying that it is worse to thin 1e6 draws by drawing every 1/1000 samples than it is to accept chains with known dependence from 1000 draws?  how about 1 sample each from 1e3 chains? My intuition is way off here, so if you can point me to some reference materials that speak to this I'd really appreciate it.
> > >
> > > Even if I generate the linear combinations as quantities within STAN, I'm not sure I'm safe to trust MC standard error. If the draws are correlated it cannot be safe unless the chains are long enough that that the tails of all the interesting quantities are evenly sampled!

> > > So, for now, I've updated my my position to think I may not have sampled enough so that the linear combinations of interest are evenly sampled. > > > Best regards

> > > > > I am concluding that thinning is still best practice for HMC (even though I read many times that thinning should not be necessary with HMC). It may not matter much, or at all, for inference on a single parameter, but it looks like it might when making inference on linear combinations of the parameters (as I am in this problem). If you disagree please let me know.

Your example seemed to mix really well though, so there was not very much within-chain dependence at all. messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Stan with small fixed standard deviation
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Stan with small fixed standard deviation
messages.body_plain:
Remember how constrained parameters are handled in Stan (as clearly
discussed in the manual): the interval (a, b) is mapped to (-infty, infty)
and sampling done on the unconstrained space.  So if you put a
uniform prior on (a, b) and expect there to be lots of posterior mass
near either boundary then that can require sampling near one of the
infinities.  Stan initializes unconstrained parameters on [-2, 2] by default
so it can take a _long_ time to converge from O(0) to O(infty).

Really we want everything to be unit scale on the unconstrained space.

And stop using uniform priors.

messages.body_plain:
Modulo the adaptation parameters all being the same —
see if the average acceptance probability and step size
are similar across chains.  If they are then outlying chains
would indicate small pathological neighborhoods that you
weren’t seeing before.  Otherwise the adaptation isn’t
converging to a consistent answer and you might have
to tweak warmup before judging any pathological regions.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Unused parameters
messages.body_plain:
If all of the parameters are non-identified then NUTS will diverge to infinity
and a warning thrown in warmup.  But if only some of the parameters are
non-identified then NUTS might terminate the trajectories prematurely and
prevent these divergences from occurring.  So we do diagnose it when we
can, but we can’t always.

messages.body_plain:
And always run multiple chains. In parallel there's really no cost to running several (preferably >= 4) rather than 1. Even if you can't parallelize for whatever reason, I'd argue that the (scientific) cost of running them sequentially (even for really slow models) is infinitely smaller than the cost of unknowingly using invalid estimates.

Of course this doesn't apply if you're doing it for educational purposes (e.g. to show that multiple chains are required in order to identify certain pathologies when doing MCMC).

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Rhat on a single chain
messages.body_plain:
It would be a cool feature like this: stan would monitor the effective
sample size during sampling (at least sporadically). Whenever the sample
is sufficiently large, a new chain is started. The user would specify
the number of threads and the desired overall sample size. Stan then
would do something like this:

c1 |-----|-------|-----|-------|--------|
c2 |---|---------|-------|---|--------|
c3 |-----|-------|-----|-------|------|
c4 |-----|-----|---------|---------|---|

E.g., ~4 serial chains in 4 threads

While currently it does something like this:

c1 |---------------------------------|
c2 |---------------------------------|
c3 |---------------------------------|
c4 |---------------------------------|

The overall sample size in this case is similar, but the across chain
diagnostics weaker (probably trades for more samples per chain than
really needed).

Each in the chains in the hypothetical first case would go through the
whole adaptation and warmup business, of course.

Best regards
Jan

messages.subject: When to use hierarchies, and when to not
messages.subject_clean: When to use hierarchies, and when to not
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am hoping that you can help me settle a debate.

My collaborators and I have data for experiments structured by the following categories (from top to bottom): genus -> species -> individual time series.

I believe that the best way to approach this is to use a hierarchical model which has 3 levels; one for each of the categories. However, my collaborators (entomologists) argue that the different species within a particular genus are so incredibly different (they use the analogy that the species within a particular genus are more different than say, lions and elephants, at a genetic level), that it does not make any sense to group them in any way. Furthermore, they argue that any 'genus-level' parameters that are estimated would be meaningless biologically, since they are averages across a range of very heterogeneous entities.

I definitely do see their point, but can't help thinking that species are categorised within a particular genus for a reason; some sort of similarity. I agree with them that the overall parameters probably won't mean much. However, I always default to using hierarchies whenever I can, due to all the benefits (reduced variance, less overfit, more parsimony etc).

I suspect it won't make all that much difference to the results (some preliminary analysis results hint at this), but wanted to see what others thought of this. Do you think that this model should be a three-level hierarchy, or independent analyses consisting of a two-level hierarchy within each genus?

Any arguments that I can leverage here would be most helpful, either way, and will ultimately lead to better justification in the paper.

Best,

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] When to use hierarchies, and when to not
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] When to use hierarchies, and when to not
messages.body_plain:
If this is a well-understood taxonomic group, then the genus ought to consist of species that are all more closely related to one another than to any other species, as the members of each species are more closely related to one another than they are to any other species. That would tend to argue for treating it hierarchically. OTOH, many groups have not been revised thoroughly and the taxonomic structure may not reflect the phylogeny as well as one might like, which could argue against it in some situations. In the third hand, not all biologists have really embraced cladistic taxonomy (naming groups based on relatedness) and the importance of controlling for the effects of shared ancestry in such analyses. In that case, you either fight wit the biologists or defer to their specialized knowledge.

If it's a particularly speciose group with lots of phylogenetic structure, and there are good published estimates of phylogenetic distance, it might make sense to incorporate that into your model. There are a few common approaches to phylogenetically-informed analysis which should be adaptable to your model.

In terms of interpreting the parameter estimates at the genus level, in an analysis fully incorporating the effects of phylogeny, the genus-level estimate ought to be something like an estimate of the common ancestor's character state. Whether such a thing is meaningful in this instance I couldn't say, but in general it seems like it should be. messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] When to use hierarchies, and when to not
messages.body_plain:
Hi, I’m cc-ing Lizzie because this is her bailiwick, but from a statistical point of view, if you use a grouping factor that’s irrelevant, then it shouldn’t matter much in the analysis.  That is, you could include a variance component for genus, and it shouldn’t really hurt you if genus doesn’t really matter for your purposes.  So you could include it, or you could do the analysis both ways and it probably won’t matter.  But the one thing you _wouldn’t_ want to do, I think, is a separate two-level model for each genus.  There’s information to be shared between genuses.  Especially if genus doesn’t matter—then you’d _really_ want to be combining across them.

But let’s step back for a moment.  Why do we do hierarchical models?  Why include grouping in the analysis?  Because if we don’t have enough local data (i.e., if we have noisy time series, in this example), we want to do partial pooling to get better, more reasonable estimates.  So . . . if your colleagues think that partial pooling across species within genus is a waste of time, then that’s fine.  But then maybe there’s another model that could be fit, using some other characteristics of the species.  To the extent that you can group the species a priori into reasonable categories, or to the extent that you can construct good species-level predictors, your partial pooling will be more effective.

A

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] When to use hierarchies, and when to not
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] When to use hierarchies, and when to not
messages.body_plain:
Hi Andrew and Ben,

The modern way to compare species is to incorporate the evolutionary relationships as a prior covariance matrix in a mixed-effects model, either on random effects associated with species (G level) or residuals (R level). Species are real entities (distinct, non-interbreeding populations) but genera are not: they are subjective artificial classifications built by taxonomists that may or may not have any basis in biology. The solution is to work with the evolutionary relationships (the phylogeny) directly, and forget about the biological classification.

Cheers,

Simon.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] When to use hierarchies, and when to not
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] When to use hierarchies, and when to not
messages.body_plain:
Hierarchical models in absolutely no way imply a causal structure,
so a phylogenetic relation is absolutely not necessary.  It may be
helpful, but in many cases is may not.  For example, consider
some model that depends on vision — if you assume that the
eye evolved independently then species in very different branches
of phylogenetic trees may have similar responses to vision-based
observables which motivates an entirely different hierarchical structure.

The hierarchy represents similarities in the observations and
consequently can only be justified as such.  Even if genera are
artificial classifications they can imply good hierarchical structure
if the classification strategies consider observable behaviors.
And phylogenetic clustering requires knowing the correct
phylogenetic tree which is itself a huge uncertain problem.

And, as Andrew notes, even if there are no similarities between
the groups the hierarchical model will learn that and shouldn’t
penalize you that much.  Plus any residual bias can actually
improve your estimates even when the groups are IID (a la
James-Stein estimation).

Ben

This actually is my bailiwick! In the past two weeks I have had two such similar debates. I have two conflicting views -- on the first side I find it interesting that your colleagues are fully behind the species concept but seem to think genus is completely irrelevant. Though I can understand that view a little I suspect the systematists who came up with the arthropods' genera may be offended by this (or for this particular group it could well be that the genus level classifications are a mess and poorly done currently). I wonder if there is some other taxonomic level they would be comfortable with such as family. Lions and elephants are actually pretty similar once you start comparing them with komodo dragons and earthworms, for example, and even I can tell a beetle from an insect.

Then to echo Andrew and go in the other direction, if your colleagues really think genus is irrelevant, or worse, poorly defined for these groups just now such that species A is in genus 1 but really belongs in genus 2 then you would be pooling in a way that could give you less biologically accurate estimates. In line with Andrew I would wonder if there are other characteristics you could group by.

In my own experiences we sometimes (1) skip all taxonomy above species and actually don't partially pool species together even because we don't want one species influencing the other too much (and, in last week's example we realized we had missing data for some species that varied by treatment which would make the pooling effect especially strong for some species with the most unique treatment effects), (2) use distances from a phylogenetic tree instead of categorical levels (but then I echo that phylogenies are their own balls of wax to start batting at and evaluating) and (3) worry about how species can often be confounded with other effects, like site or who did the study. It sounds like from the below you might be in the realm of (3) perhaps.

HTH and any other opinions, including on what I do, welcome. I find it's a messy area!

L

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] A question on convergence
messages.body_plain:
I’ve said it before I’ll say it again THERE IS NO SUCH THING AS _AN_
AUTOCORRELATION IN A MARKOV CHAIN.

Consider a target distribution, pi, a Markov transition, T, and some
function whose expectation we want to take, f.  Asymptotically

\lim_{N \rightarrow \infty} \sum_{n = 1}^{N} f(x_{n}) = E_{pi} [ f ].

Given some nicer regularity conditions (usually we need at least
geometric ergodicity) then the MCMC estimator

\sum_{n = 1}^{N} f(x_{n})

converges in distribution to

N( E_{pi} [ f ], sigma^{2} / ESS )

where sigma is the true variance of f under pi and ESS is the
effective sample size,

ESS = N / (1 + \sum_{l = 1}^{\infty} rho_{l} ),

where l is the lag-l autocorrelation of f.  This is called the MCMC
central limit theorem.

The important thing to keep in mind here is that the autocorrelations
depend on f!  There is no way to define a canonical autocorrelation
for the chain itself.  So some functions can have large autocorrelations
and some can have small autocorrelations _in the same chain_.
Intuitively, the more a function varies the more it relies on the fine
details of the target distribution, the longer it will need the Markov
chain to converge, and the larger the autocorrelations will be.

Your PCA is just constructing a function as sensitive to the spatial
scales as possible, yielding larger autocorrelations but that has
absolutely nothing to do with the other expectations and does not
indicate that those ESS calculations are wrong.

The only caveat is that we have access to only ESS _estimates_
and we have to worry about how accurate those estimates can
be.  But these kinds of analyses do not provide any such utility.

Finally, assuming that the MCMC CLT holds you define the number
of steps you need by first determining how well you need to estimate
E_{pi} [ f ] and then running until

MCSE = sqrt{ sigma^{2} / ESS }

achieves that desired precision.  MCSE is printed along with the
other Stan summaries.

messages.body_plain:
I have toyed around with Gaussian processes with phylogenetic distance as an input in order to allow for correlation among species as it relates to evolutionary history. For prediction, these GP models are outperforming models with hierarchical structure based only on taxonomy (genus, family, order, etc.). Conveniently, previous work (e.g., Hansen and Martins 1996 <http://www.researchgate.net/profile/Emilia_Martins/publication/258872200_Translating_between_microevolutionary_process_and_macroevolutionary_patterns_the_correlation_structure_of_interspecific_data/links/00b7d5294c2d28e8e5000000.pdf>) points to correlation functions with mechanistic support. I haven't been accounting for uncertainty in the phylogeny, however, though such approaches do exist (e.g., de Villemereuil et al. 2012 <http://www.biomedcentral.com/1471-2148/12/102/>).

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] When to use hierarchies, and when to not
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] When to use hierarchies, and when to not
messages.body_plain:
On 30/10/15 21:52, Michael Betancourt wrote:

> Hierarchical models in absolutely no way imply a causal structure,
> so a phylogenetic relation is absolutely not necessary.  It may be
> helpful, but in many cases is may not.  For example, consider
> some model that depends on vision — if you assume that the
> eye evolved independently then species in very different branches
> of phylogenetic trees may have similar responses to vision-based

> observables which motivates an entirely different hierarchical structure.Tj

That's the point. A phylogenetic model explicitly accounts for non-independence in the data due to common ancestry. Organisms can be similar due to common ancestry OR convergence. If convergence is your hypothesis, there are methods for testing for that, although how to do it correctly is a topic of current research.

>
> The hierarchy represents similarities in the observations and
> consequently can only be justified as such.  Even if genera are
> artificial classifications they can imply good hierarchical structure
> if the classification strategies consider observable behaviors.
> And phylogenetic clustering requires knowing the correct
> phylogenetic tree which is itself a huge uncertain problem.

If the genera are monophyletic, then you may not be far wrong. But it completely ignores the intra-generic lack of independence, and it also treats each genus equally. Some genera will be more closely related to each other than others. Let's be clear. You cannot avoid making a phylogenetic assumption in these kinds of models. The taxonomic approach implies a certain correlation structure for the data: All genera are monophyletic and assumed to arise at the same time, and independently of each other, and all species within a genus are assumed to arise at the same time and independently of each other. We know that this assumption is always wrong. Why build models which we know to be wrong on such an important aspect of the data? The only objective way to correctly model the phylogenetic independence is to use the phylogeny. Now, all models are wrong etc. But why be deliberately wrong by using a taxonomic hierarchical structure?

Bayesian methods are IDEAL for incorporating phylogenetic uncertainty. We have methods for that. (See the citation of one of my papers in a different part of the thread.)

>
> And, as Andrew notes, even if there are no similarities between
> the groups the hierarchical model will learn that and shouldn’t
> penalize you that much.

I agree. It may be that the phylogeny might not add much to the analysis. But that is always an empirical question and not an argument for not using a phylogenetic model when you suspect that lack of independence due to phylogenetic relationships may be a problem. You can't really know that in advance.

>  Plus any residual bias can actually
> improve your estimates even when the groups are IID (a la
> James-Stein estimation).

But we _know_ that the groups are NOT IID. I'm not arguing against a heirarchical structure to the model. I'm just emphasising that using the taxonomy is the wrong way to do it.

Cheers,

Simon.

>
> On Oct 30, 2015, at 5:47 AM, Simon Blomberg <s.blo...@uq.edu.au> wrote:

Species are real entities (distinct, non-interbreeding populations) but genera are not: they are subjective artificial classifications built by taxonomists that may or may not have any basis in biology. The solution is to work with the evolutionary relationships (the phylogeny) directly, and forget about the biological classification.

That is, you could include a variance component for genus, and it shouldn’t really hurt you if genus doesn’t really matter for your purposes.  So you could include it, or you could do the analysis both ways and it probably won’t matter.  But the one thing you _wouldn’t_ want to do, I think, is a separate two-level model for each genus.  There’s information to be shared between genuses.  Especially if genus doesn’t matter—then you’d _really_ want to be combining across them.

But then maybe there’s another model that could be fit, using some other characteristics of the species.  To the extent that you can group the species a priori into reasonable categories, or to the extent that you can construct good species-level predictors, your partial pooling will be more effective.

I have two conflicting views -- on the first side I find it interesting that your colleagues are fully behind the species concept but seem to think genus is completely irrelevant. Though I can understand that view a little I suspect the systematists who came up with the arthropods' genera may be offended by this (or for this particular group it could well be that the genus level classifications are a mess and poorly done currently). I wonder if there is some other taxonomic level they would be comfortable with such as family. Lions and elephants are actually pretty similar once you start comparing them with komodo dragons and earthworms, for example, and even I can tell a beetle from an insect.

I don't see why biologists should care about systematists' feelings about their classifications. To paraphrase one of your presidents, "It's the phylogeny, stupid!". And moving to family-level data just moves the exact same problem up the hierarchy. Also, note that you have already made a phylogenetic mistake: beetles ARE insects.

>
> Then to echo Andrew and go in the other direction, if your colleagues really think genus is irrelevant, or worse, poorly defined for these groups just now such that species A is in genus 1 but really belongs in genus 2 then you would be pooling in a way that could give you less biologically accurate estimates. In line with Andrew I would wonder if there are other characteristics you could group by.

You could, for example classify species into ecological guilds (a guild is a group of possibly unrelated species that inhabit similar niches). But that doesn't get around the problem of phylogenetic lack of independence in the data.

>
> In my own experiences we sometimes (1) skip all taxonomy above species and actually don't partially pool species together even because we don't want one species influencing the other too much (and, in last week's example we realized we had missing data for some species that varied by treatment which would make the pooling effect especially strong for some species with the most unique treatment effects),

Not using any phylogenetic information at all, treating species as IID is perhaps the worst thing you could do. There is a strong analogy between time series and spatial data here. We would not treat time series as IID (no temporal autocorrelation), or spatial data without considering spatial autocorrelation. We should have the same respect for cross-species data. We should incorporate phylogenetic information on cross-species correlations, or at least entertain the idea that phylogenetic covariance could be a problem. There are some situations in which phylogenetic information could conceivably be ignored.  For the time series analogy, we might pretend that our data are IID if the time series is short. Or for spatial data where the data are very far apart in space, making the IID assumption more plausible. So for small data sets or data sets where the phylogenetic covariance is thought to be extremely small, e.g. comparing phyla, it is possible that phylogenetic effects could be neglected. But that is an empirical question.

> (2) use distances from a phylogenetic tree instead of categorical levels (but then I echo that phylogenies are their own balls of wax to start batting at and evaluating)

Then collaborate with a systematist to work out the phylogeny! (I find it ironic that I say this, as I often exhort systematists to collaborate with statisticians!)

> and (3) worry about how species can often be confounded with other effects, like site or who did the study.

Yes, these are important issues in any comparative analysis.

Cheers,

Simon.

Gaussian processes are currently the standard approach to analysing
cross-species data. Essentially, you need a model of evolution for your
traits. The most common models are Brownian motion and the
Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process (both Gaussian). In both cases there is a
simple relationship between the branch lengths on the phylogeny and the
covariance structure for the data. I don't know about mixture models in
this context.

> That's the point. A phylogenetic model explicitly accounts for non-independence in the data due to common ancestry. Organisms can be similar due to common ancestry OR convergence. If convergence is your hypothesis, there are methods for testing for that, although how to do it correctly is a topic of current research.

Yeah, you are missing the point entirely.  As I said before,
a phylogenetic model is a causal model — but the observational
correlations between species need not be causal.  Hierarchical
structure is statistical so it doesn’t need nor really care about
whether any correlations are causal, which is why they are so
amazingly powerful and widely applicable.

And, once again, there is no real cost of adding hierarchical
structure that’s not there other than increased computation
(the hierarchical model will converge to an IID model if
necessitated by the data).  Another reason why they are so
awesome.

> If the genera are monophyletic, then you may not be far wrong. But it completely ignores the intra-generic lack of independence, and it also treats each genus equally. Some genera will be more closely related to each other than others. Let's be clear. You cannot avoid making a phylogenetic assumption in these kinds of models. The taxonomic approach implies a certain correlation structure for the data: All genera are monophyletic and assumed to arise at the same time, and independently of each other, and all species within a genus are assumed to arise at the same time and independently of each other. We know that this assumption is always wrong. Why build models which we know to be wrong on such an important aspect of the data? The only objective way to correctly model the phylogenetic independence is to use the phylogeny. Now, all models are wrong etc. But why be deliberately wrong by using a taxonomic hierarchical structure?

Because we might not care a lick about the phylogenetic
structure!  Taxonomic structure can capture useful correlations
— if you think otherwise than criticize the particular choice
of taxonomy relative to a given observational model, but
blanket criticizing taxonomies is equivalent to blanket
criticizing hierarchical models in general which are in
general not cause relationships.

Can phylogenetics provide useful motivation for building
statistical models?  Absolutely.  Are they necessary and
sufficient for all statistical analyses?  No way.

> Bayesian methods are IDEAL for incorporating phylogenetic uncertainty. We have methods for that. (See the citation of one of my papers in a different part of the thread.)

Yeah, they are.  Or they will be we have any idea how to
effectively explore and sample from tree spaces with
corresponding guarantees/validation methods/diagnostics
that we can represent the true posterior uncertainty with
any fidelity.  Topological real talk.

> I agree. It may be that the phylogeny might not add much to the analysis. But that is always an empirical question and not an argument for not using a phylogenetic model when you suspect that lack of independence due to phylogenetic relationships may be a problem. You can't really know that in advance.

No, no, no.  Again, we’re not talking about phylogenetics.
The point is that even if you don’t like a chosen taxonomic
structure then you don’t have to worry about the fit because
the hierarchical model will learn the independence of the
groups

> But we _know_ that the groups are NOT IID.

If they’re not IID then there’s some correlation that can be
learned and utilized for improved inferences!  It doesn’t
matter what causes the correlation — once again hierarchical
structure need not be causal!  Have I mentioned that before?

But you _should_ care! You should care for the same reason as that you would care about temporal autocorrelation in time series, spatial autocorrelation in spatial data, pedigree information in genetic models etc. The phylogeny is the only way to incorporate that information in cross-species data. I am criticising taxonomy in general because they a) don't represent anything like phylogenetic hierarchical structure. To the extent that taxonomies are useful is only because of some (perhaps accidental) similarities to the underlying phylogeny and b) they are not objective. I am _not_ criticising hierarchical models in general. I use them all the time, and I think Bayes is the best way to implement these models. It's just the structure of the hierarchy that I am arguing should be based on the phylogeny.

> statistical models?  Absolutely.  Are they necessary and
> sufficient for all statistical analyses?  No way.

>
> Yeah, they are.  Or they will be we have any idea how to
> effectively explore and sample from tree spaces with
> corresponding guarantees/validation methods/diagnostics
> that we can represent the true posterior uncertainty with
> any fidelity.  Topological real talk.

We do have methods for sampling from tree space. Diagnostics for that sample are harder because trees are complicated beasts and there may be many ways in which our sample may be unusual. What does it mean to converge in tree space? Not clear to me. This is a current topic of research. Input from topologists would be welcome.

>
> > I agree. It may be that the phylogeny might not add much to the analysis. But that is always an empirical question and not an argument for not using a phylogenetic model when you suspect that lack of independence due to phylogenetic relationships may be a problem. You can't really know that in advance.
>
> No, no, no.  Again, we’re not talking about phylogenetics.
> The point is that even if you don’t like a chosen taxonomic
> structure then you don’t have to worry about the fit because
> the hierarchical model will learn the independence of the
> groups

And that lack of independence can be represented a priori by the phylogeny. In fact, the phylogenetic information is the only objective way of incorporating that information. Whether that information contributes to the posterior is then an empirical question as the model learns.

>
> > But we _know_ that the groups are NOT IID.
>
> If they’re not IID then there’s some correlation that can be
> learned and utilized for improved inferences!

Yep, described by the phylogeny!

> It doesn’t
> matter what causes the correlation — once again hierarchical
> structure need not be causal!  Have I mentioned that before?

Yes. Yes you have. Models need not be causal. But the lack of independence in the data should still be considered. The taxonomy won't usually cut it. A good phylogeny will.

messages.body_plain:
Without specifying the observable, there are some objective facts.

a) Taxonomical structure may be based on previous observations
    that may be compatible with new measurements, hence a quite
    good motivation for a hierarchical prior.

b) Even if the hierarchical structure is chosen poorly the model will
    adapt and inferences will largely remain valid.

c) Even if there is some “objective” phylogenetic structure, it need
    not manifest in the observables and hence need not be relevant
    to a hierarchical model.

d) Known phylogenetic structures depend on data models, models
    which are built out of assumptions, assumptions which are in
    no way “objective”.

e) On top of that, even state-of-the-art phylogenetic MCMC methods
    are extremely limited.  So even if there was an “objective" model
    we wouldn’t be able to use it to construct the necessary inferences
    to pick out the corresponding “objective” phylogenetic trees compatible
    with the data.

So the statement that "phylogenetic trees are objective and known a priori"
and "always the correct hierarchical structure” are both incorrect.  In a real
problem using neither taxonomical structure or phylogentic structure will
lead to poor inferences.  One may certainly be better, but which is better
depends very strongly on the details of a given model and hence no
approach can be determined “correct” for all models.

Again the original question was not “should I use a taxonomical hierarchy
or phylogenetic hierarchy” but rather “will using a taxonomical hierarchy
lead to poor inferences.”  The latter is absolutely not.  End of answer.
